Week 13 · Phase 4: Advanced Topics

Generative Models II: Diffusion, Flows, and Autoregressive Models

Denoising diffusion from first principles (forward process, reverse process, the variational bound and the epsilon-prediction loss), noise schedules and v-prediction, score matching and the SDE/probability-flow view, DDIM and fast samplers, classifier and classifier-free guidance, latent diffusion with U-Net and DiT backbones, normalizing flows and autoregressive models, a comparison of all generative families, and the societal risks of synthetic media. The lab trains a small class-conditional DDPM on MNIST and explores sampling steps and guidance.

84 min read3 interactive demos13 figures15 code blocks11 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Write the DDPM forward process, derive the closed form q(xt∣x0)q(x_t\mid x_0)q(xt​∣x0​), and explain why it makes training cheap.
  • Derive the reverse-process posterior q(xt−1∣xt,x0)q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)q(xt−1​∣xt​,x0​), the variational bound, and the simplified ϵ\epsilonϵ-prediction loss, and say what the simplification throws away.
  • Compare linear and cosine noise schedules through αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​ and the signal-to-noise ratio, and convert between ϵ\epsilonϵ-, x0x_0x0​-, and vvv-parameterizations.
  • Define the score function, derive denoising score matching, and show that ϵ\epsilonϵ-prediction is score estimation up to a scale.
  • State the forward SDE, the reverse-time SDE and the probability-flow ODE, and explain how DDPM and DDIM are discretizations of them.
  • Derive classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance and explain the quality/diversity trade-off controlled by the guidance scale.
  • Explain latent diffusion, cross-attention conditioning, and the architectural differences between U-Net and DiT denoisers.
  • Describe normalizing flows (change of variables, coupling layers) and autoregressive models (PixelCNN, WaveNet, Transformers over tokens), and place all five generative families in one comparison.
  • Discuss deepfakes, provenance (C2PA), watermarking and other risks of generative media with technical precision.
  • Train a class-conditional DDPM on MNIST and run sampling-step and guidance experiments.

Week 12 ended with a tension. VAEs train stably and cover the data, but their samples are blurry; GANs make sharp samples but are hard to train and can drop modes. Between roughly 2020 and 2022 a third family closed most of that gap and then took over image, audio and video generation: diffusion models. The idea is almost embarrassingly simple. Take a data point and add a little Gaussian noise, again and again, until nothing but noise is left. Then train a neural network to undo one small step of that corruption. Generating data means starting from pure noise and applying the learned denoiser many times.

Why does that work so much better than asking a network to produce an image in one shot? Because the hard problem (go from noise to a sharp, globally coherent image) is split into hundreds of easy ones (remove a little noise from a slightly-noisy image), and each easy problem is a plain regression with a stable, well-behaved loss. This week derives the model from three angles that turn out to be the same thing: a variational latent-variable model (a hierarchical VAE with a fixed encoder), a denoising / score-matching model (a network that points toward higher-density regions), and a differential equation (a continuous flow that carries noise to data). Then we make the sampler fast (DDIM), make it controllable (guidance, text conditioning), make it scale (latent diffusion, Transformers), look at the two other likelihood-based families (flows and autoregressive models), compare everything, and finish with the societal side. The lab trains a small DDPM on MNIST from scratch.

The diffusion idea in one picture

Two Markov chains, one fixed and one learned:

  • The forward (noising) process q(xt∣xt−1)q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})q(xt​∣xt−1​) for t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,Tt=1,…,T turns a data point x0∼pdatax_0\sim p_\text{data}x0​∼pdata​ into a nearly-pure-Gaussian xTx_TxT​. It is designed by hand and has no learnable parameters.
  • The reverse (denoising) process pθ(xt−1∣xt)p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)pθ​(xt−1​∣xt​) goes from xT∼N(0,I)x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)xT​∼N(0,I) back to x0x_0x0​. A neural network parameterizes it. If the forward steps are small, the true reverse step is also (close to) a Gaussian, which is why a Gaussian with a learned mean is a reasonable model of it, not just a convenient one.

The model was introduced by Sohl-Dickstein, Weiss, Maheswaranathan and Ganguli in 2015 (inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics), then sat nearly unnoticed until Ho, Jain and Abbeel (2020) showed with a simple loss, a U-Net and a careful schedule that it could rival GANs on CIFAR-10 and 256x256 LSUN images. In parallel, Song and Ermon (2019) developed noise-conditional score networks from the score-matching tradition. Song et al. (2021) then showed the two lines are one theory.

Two roads to the same place

The thermodynamic road: Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) proposed learning to reverse a diffusion process. The score-matching road: Hyvarinen (2005) introduced score matching, Vincent (2011) connected it to denoising autoencoders, and Song and Ermon (2019) trained a network on many noise levels and sampled with Langevin dynamics. Ho et al. (2020) unified the practicalities (a simple ϵ\epsilonϵ-prediction loss, a U-Net backbone), and Song et al. (2021) framed both with stochastic differential equations. Modern systems (Stable Diffusion, Imagen, DALL-E 2 and 3, video models) are descendants of this merged line. Keep both vocabularies in your head: papers use them interchangeably.

The forward process and its closed form

One step of noising

Fix a variance schedule β1,…,βT∈(0,1)\beta_1,\dots,\beta_T\in(0,1)β1​,…,βT​∈(0,1) (small numbers, typically from 10−410^{-4}10−4 to 0.020.020.02 in the original paper). The forward step is

q(xt∣xt−1)=N ⁣(xt; 1−βt xt−1, βtI),i.e.xt=1−βt xt−1+βt ϵt,ϵt∼N(0,I).q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal N\!\big(x_t;\ \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\big), \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad x_t=\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon_{t},\quad \epsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I).q(xt​∣xt−1​)=N(xt​; 1−βt​​xt−1​, βt​I),i.e.xt​=1−βt​​xt−1​+βt​​ϵt​,ϵt​∼N(0,I).

Intuition: shrink the signal slightly (by 1−βt\sqrt{1-\beta_t}1−βt​​) and add a little fresh noise (variance βt\beta_tβt​). The shrinking matters. If you only added noise the variance would grow without bound; with the shrink factor, the process is variance preserving: if xt−1x_{t-1}xt−1​ has unit variance per coordinate, so does xtx_txt​, because (1−βt)⋅1+βt=1(1-\beta_t)\cdot 1+\beta_t=1(1−βt​)⋅1+βt​=1. Eventually the stationary distribution is N(0,I)\mathcal N(0,I)N(0,I), whatever the data looked like.

Write αt=1−βt\alpha_t=1-\beta_tαt​=1−βt​ and αˉt=∏s=1tαs\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_sαˉt​=∏s=1t​αs​.

The closed-form noising distribution

Derivation: jumping straight to step ttt

Substitute the one-step recursion into itself:

xt=αt xt−1+1−αt ϵt=αt(αt−1 xt−2+1−αt−1 ϵt−1)+1−αt ϵt=αtαt−1 xt−2+αt(1−αt−1) ϵt−1+1−αt ϵt⏟sum of two independent Gaussians.\begin{aligned} x_t&=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_t\\ &=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\big(\sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_{t-2}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t-1}}\,\epsilon_{t-1}\big)+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_t\\ &=\sqrt{\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_{t-2}+\underbrace{\sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})}\,\epsilon_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_t}_{\text{sum of two independent Gaussians}} . \end{aligned}xt​​=αt​​xt−1​+1−αt​​ϵt​=αt​​(αt−1​​xt−2​+1−αt−1​​ϵt−1​)+1−αt​​ϵt​=αt​αt−1​​xt−2​+sum of two independent Gaussiansαt​(1−αt−1​)​ϵt−1​+1−αt​​ϵt​​​.​

The sum of independent zero-mean Gaussians is a zero-mean Gaussian whose variance is the sum of the variances: αt(1−αt−1)+(1−αt)=1−αtαt−1\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})+(1-\alpha_t)=1-\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}αt​(1−αt−1​)+(1−αt​)=1−αt​αt−1​. So the noise term equals 1−αtαt−1 ϵˉ\sqrt{1-\alpha_t\alpha_{t-1}}\,\bar\epsilon1−αt​αt−1​​ϵˉ for a fresh ϵˉ∼N(0,I)\bar\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)ϵˉ∼N(0,I). Repeating the argument down to x0x_0x0​ (a one-line induction) gives

 q(xt∣x0)=N ⁣(xt; αˉt x0, (1−αˉt)I),xt=αˉt x0+1−αˉt ϵ,  ϵ∼N(0,I). \boxed{\,q(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N\!\big(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t)I\big),\qquad x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\ \ \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).\,}q(xt​∣x0​)=N(xt​; αˉt​​x0​, (1−αˉt​)I),xt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ,  ϵ∼N(0,I).​

Three things to appreciate:

  1. Training is cheap. To get a training example at a random step ttt you do not simulate ttt steps; you draw ϵ\epsilonϵ and apply one formula. This is what makes diffusion training a plain supervised regression.
  2. αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​ is the whole story. The "signal" weight is αˉt\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}αˉt​​ and the "noise" weight is 1−αˉt\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}1−αˉt​​. Their squares sum to one (variance preserving). At αˉt≈1\bar\alpha_t\approx1αˉt​≈1 you see almost clean data; at αˉt≈0\bar\alpha_t\approx0αˉt​≈0 almost pure noise. Many papers drop βt\beta_tβt​ entirely and define a model directly through αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​.
  3. Signal-to-noise ratio. SNR(t)=αˉt/(1−αˉt)\mathrm{SNR}(t)=\bar\alpha_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)SNR(t)=αˉt​/(1−αˉt​) is the ratio of signal power to noise power. It decreases monotonically in ttt. Its logarithm will turn out to be the natural "time" variable (later).

The NumPy code below builds the original linear schedule, checks the closed form against explicitly simulating ttt steps, and prints how fast the signal dies.

pythonforward_closed_form.py
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T = 1000
betas = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)           # linear schedule from Ho et al. (2020)
alphas = 1.0 - betas
alpha_bar = np.cumprod(alphas)               # alpha_bar[t-1] is \bar{alpha}_t

# 1) closed form vs explicit simulation, for a 1-D data point x0 = 2.0 at t = 300
x0, t, n = 2.0, 300, 200_000
x = np.full(n, x0)
for s in range(t):                           # t explicit noising steps
    x = np.sqrt(alphas[s]) * x + np.sqrt(betas[s]) * rng.standard_normal(n)
ab = alpha_bar[t - 1]
print(f"simulated   mean={x.mean():.4f} var={x.var():.4f}")
print(f"closed form mean={np.sqrt(ab) * x0:.4f} var={1 - ab:.4f}")

# 2) how quickly does the signal die?
for t in [1, 100, 250, 500, 750, 1000]:
    ab = alpha_bar[t - 1]
    print(f"t={t:4d}  alpha_bar={ab:.5f}  signal std={np.sqrt(ab):.3f}  noise std={np.sqrt(1-ab):.3f}  SNR={ab/(1-ab):.4g}")

The reverse process and its posterior

Sampling needs the reverse conditionals q(xt−1∣xt)q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)q(xt−1​∣xt​). Applying Bayes' rule to them requires the marginal over all possible data x0x_0x0​, which is exactly the intractable thing we want to learn. Two facts rescue us.

Fact 1 (small steps). When βt\beta_tβt​ is small, the true reverse step q(xt−1∣xt)q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)q(xt−1​∣xt​) is approximately Gaussian (Feller, 1949, for diffusion processes; this is what makes the whole construction legitimate). So we model pθ(xt−1∣xt)=N(xt−1;μθ(xt,t),Σθ(xt,t))p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\mathcal N(x_{t-1};\mu_\theta(x_t,t),\Sigma_\theta(x_t,t))pθ​(xt−1​∣xt​)=N(xt−1​;μθ​(xt​,t),Σθ​(xt​,t)).

Fact 2 (conditioning on x0x_0x0​ makes it exact). If we also condition on the clean data point, the reverse step is tractable and exactly Gaussian. We will use it as the training target.

Derivation: the posterior q(xt−1∣xt,x0)q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)q(xt−1​∣xt​,x0​)

By Bayes and the Markov property, q(xt−1∣xt,x0)=q(xt∣xt−1) q(xt−1∣x0)q(xt∣x0) ∝ q(xt∣xt−1) q(xt−1∣x0).q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=\frac{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)}{q(x_t\mid x_0)}\ \propto\ q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0).q(xt−1​∣xt​,x0​)=q(xt​∣x0​)q(xt​∣xt−1​)q(xt−1​∣x0​)​ ∝ q(xt​∣xt−1​)q(xt−1​∣x0​). Both factors on the right are Gaussians in xt−1x_{t-1}xt−1​, so the product is Gaussian. Collect the exponent (all terms in xt−1x_{t-1}xt−1​, per coordinate): −12[(xt−αtxt−1)2βt+(xt−1−αˉt−1x0)21−αˉt−1]=−12[(αtβt+11−αˉt−1)⏟1/β~txt−12−2(αtβtxt+αˉt−11−αˉt−1x0)xt−1+const].-\tfrac12\Big[\tfrac{(x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1})^2}{\beta_t}+\tfrac{(x_{t-1}-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0)^2}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\Big] =-\tfrac12\Big[\underbrace{\Big(\tfrac{\alpha_t}{\beta_t}+\tfrac1{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\Big)}_{1/\tilde\beta_t}x_{t-1}^2-2\Big(\tfrac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}{\beta_t}x_t+\tfrac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}}{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0\Big)x_{t-1}+\text{const}\Big].−21​[βt​(xt​−αt​​xt−1​)2​+1−αˉt−1​(xt−1​−αˉt−1​​x0​)2​]=−21​[1/β~​t​(βt​αt​​+1−αˉt−1​1​)​​xt−12​−2(βt​αt​​​xt​+1−αˉt−1​αˉt−1​​​x0​)xt−1​+const]. Matching to −12β~(xt−1−μ~)2-\tfrac1{2\tilde\beta}(x_{t-1}-\tilde\mu)^2−2β~​1​(xt−1​−μ~​)2 gives the variance and mean β~t=1−αˉt−11−αˉt βt,μ~t(xt,x0)=αˉt−1 βt1−αˉt x0+αt (1−αˉt−1)1−αˉt xt.\tilde\beta_t=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\beta_t,\qquad \tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t .β~​t​=1−αˉt​1−αˉt−1​​βt​,μ~​t​(xt​,x0​)=1−αˉt​αˉt−1​​βt​​x0​+1−αˉt​αt​​(1−αˉt−1​)​xt​. (The simplification of 1/β~t1/\tilde\beta_t1/β~​t​ uses αt(1−αˉt−1)+βt=1−αˉt\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})+\beta_t=1-\bar\alpha_tαt​(1−αˉt−1​)+βt​=1−αˉt​.) Now substitute x0=(xt−1−αˉt ϵ)/αˉtx_0=\big(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\big)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x0​=(xt​−1−αˉt​​ϵ)/αˉt​​ from the closed form; after algebra the xtx_txt​ coefficient collapses and  μ~t=1αt(xt−βt1−αˉt ϵ) \boxed{\ \tilde\mu_t=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon\Big)\ } μ~​t​=αt​​1​(xt​−1−αˉt​​βt​​ϵ) ​ where ϵ\epsilonϵ is the noise that was used to produce xtx_txt​ from x0x_0x0​.

Read the boxed formula as a recipe: to step backwards, take xtx_txt​, subtract the (scaled) noise that was added, and rescale. The only thing the network needs to supply is that noise ϵ\epsilonϵ. This is the origin of ϵ\epsilonϵ-prediction.

Let us check the posterior coefficients numerically before building on them.

pythonposterior_check.py
import numpy as np
T = 1000
betas = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T); alphas = 1 - betas
ab = np.cumprod(alphas); ab_prev = np.concatenate([[1.0], ab[:-1]])

t = 400 - 1                                   # 0-based index of step 400
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x0 = rng.standard_normal(5); eps = rng.standard_normal(5)
xt = np.sqrt(ab[t]) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - ab[t]) * eps

# posterior mean from the (x0, xt) form
c0 = np.sqrt(ab_prev[t]) * betas[t] / (1 - ab[t])
ct = np.sqrt(alphas[t]) * (1 - ab_prev[t]) / (1 - ab[t])
mu_a = c0 * x0 + ct * xt
# posterior mean from the epsilon form
mu_b = (xt - betas[t] / np.sqrt(1 - ab[t]) * eps) / np.sqrt(alphas[t])
print(np.abs(mu_a - mu_b).max())              # ~1e-16: the two forms agree
print("posterior variance beta_tilde =", (1 - ab_prev[t]) / (1 - ab[t]) * betas[t], " vs beta_t =", betas[t])

The variational bound and the simplified loss

Diffusion is a latent-variable model pθ(x0)=∫pθ(x0:T) dx1:Tp_\theta(x_0)=\int p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}pθ​(x0​)=∫pθ​(x0:T​)dx1:T​ whose latents x1:Tx_{1:T}x1:T​ have the same dimension as the data. The inference ("encoder") distribution is the fixed forward process q(x1:T∣x0)q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)q(x1:T​∣x0​). Exactly as for the VAE of Week 12, the negative log-likelihood is bounded by the ELBO.

Derivation: the diffusion ELBO

Let pθ(x0:T)=p(xT)∏t=1Tpθ(xt−1∣xt)p_\theta(x_{0:T})=p(x_T)\prod_{t=1}^Tp_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)pθ​(x0:T​)=p(xT​)∏t=1T​pθ​(xt−1​∣xt​) with p(xT)=N(0,I)p(x_T)=\mathcal N(0,I)p(xT​)=N(0,I). Jensen's inequality gives −log⁡pθ(x0)≤Eq(x1:T∣x0)[−log⁡pθ(x0:T)q(x1:T∣x0)]=:L.-\log p_\theta(x_0)\le \E_{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\Big[-\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\Big]=:L .−logpθ​(x0​)≤Eq(x1:T​∣x0​)​[−logq(x1:T​∣x0​)pθ​(x0:T​)​]=:L. Insert the factorizations, and rewrite each forward factor with Bayes' rule using q(xt∣xt−1)=q(xt∣xt−1,x0)=q(xt−1∣xt,x0) q(xt∣x0)q(xt−1∣x0)q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=q(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_0)=\frac{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,q(x_t\mid x_0)}{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)}q(xt​∣xt−1​)=q(xt​∣xt−1​,x0​)=q(xt−1​∣x0​)q(xt−1​∣xt​,x0​)q(xt​∣x0​)​ for t≥2t\ge2t≥2. The marginal ratios telescope, leaving L=DKL ⁣(q(xT∣x0) ∥ p(xT))⏟LT+∑t=2TEq DKL ⁣(q(xt−1∣xt,x0) ∥ pθ(xt−1∣xt))⏟Lt−1 − Eqlog⁡pθ(x0∣x1)⏟L0.L=\underbrace{\KL\!\big(q(x_T\mid x_0)\,\|\,p(x_T)\big)}_{L_T} +\sum_{t=2}^{T}\underbrace{\E_q\,\KL\!\big(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\big)}_{L_{t-1}} \ \underbrace{-\ \E_q\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)}_{L_0}.L=LT​DKL​(q(xT​∣x0​)∥p(xT​))​​+t=2∑T​Lt−1​Eq​DKL​(q(xt−1​∣xt​,x0​)∥pθ​(xt−1​∣xt​))​​ L0​− Eq​logpθ​(x0​∣x1​)​​.

  • LTL_TLT​ has no parameters; it is tiny when αˉT≈0\bar\alpha_T\approx0αˉT​≈0.
  • L0L_0L0​ is a reconstruction (decoder) term for the last step.
  • Each Lt−1L_{t-1}Lt−1​ is a KL between two Gaussians: the exact posterior N(μ~t,β~tI)\mathcal N(\tilde\mu_t,\tilde\beta_tI)N(μ~​t​,β~​t​I) and the model N(μθ,σt2I)\mathcal N(\mu_\theta,\sigma_t^2I)N(μθ​,σt2​I).

If we fix the model variance to σt2\sigma_t^2σt2​ (Ho et al. use σt2=βt\sigma_t^2=\beta_tσt2​=βt​ or β~t\tilde\beta_tβ~​t​; the two behave nearly the same), the KL between equal-covariance Gaussians is a squared distance between means (compare the closed-form KL in Week 12):

Lt−1=Ex0,ϵ[12σt2∥μ~t(xt,x0)−μθ(xt,t)∥2]+const.L_{t-1}=\E_{x_0,\epsilon}\Big[\frac1{2\sigma_t^2}\big\|\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)-\mu_\theta(x_t,t)\big\|^2\Big]+\text{const}.Lt−1​=Ex0​,ϵ​[2σt2​1​​μ~​t​(xt​,x0​)−μθ​(xt​,t)​2]+const.

Now choose the parameterization of μθ\mu_\thetaμθ​ to mirror μ~t\tilde\mu_tμ~​t​, with the network predicting the noise:

μθ(xt,t)=1αt(xt−βt1−αˉt ϵθ(xt,t)) ⟹ Lt−1=Ex0,ϵ[βt22σt2 αt (1−αˉt) ∥ϵ−ϵθ(αˉtx0+1−αˉt ϵ, t)∥2].\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\Big) \ \Longrightarrow\ L_{t-1}=\E_{x_0,\epsilon}\Big[\frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\,\alpha_t\,(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\,\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\ t)\big\|^2\Big].μθ​(xt​,t)=αt​​1​(xt​−1−αˉt​​βt​​ϵθ​(xt​,t)) ⟹ Lt−1​=Ex0​,ϵ​[2σt2​αt​(1−αˉt​)βt2​​​ϵ−ϵθ​(αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ, t)​2].

The xtx_txt​ terms cancel inside μ~t−μθ\tilde\mu_t-\mu_\thetaμ~​t​−μθ​, leaving only the difference in the noise predictions. This is a weighted sum of denoising errors, with a ttt-dependent weight λt=βt2/(2σt2αt(1−αˉt))\lambda_t=\beta_t^2/(2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t))λt​=βt2​/(2σt2​αt​(1−αˉt​)). Ho et al. found that dropping the weights and sampling ttt uniformly works better in practice for sample quality:

 Lsimple(θ)=Ex0∼pdata, t∼U{1..T}, ϵ∼N(0,I)[∥ϵ−ϵθ(αˉt x0+1−αˉt ϵ, t)∥2] \boxed{\ \mathcal L_\text{simple}(\theta)=\E_{x_0\sim p_\text{data},\ t\sim\mathcal U\{1..T\},\ \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)}\Big[\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\ t\big)\big\|^2\Big]\ } Lsimple​(θ)=Ex0​∼pdata​, t∼U{1..T}, ϵ∼N(0,I)​[​ϵ−ϵθ​(αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ, t)​2] ​

What the simplification costs

The true ELBO weights are large at small ttt (low noise) and small at large ttt. Lsimple\mathcal L_\text{simple}Lsimple​ down-weights the easy, low-noise steps relative to the ELBO, which frees capacity for the harder high-noise denoising tasks that determine global structure. The price is that Lsimple\mathcal L_\text{simple}Lsimple​ is not a bound on the likelihood: models trained with it have noticeably worse log-likelihoods (in bits per dimension) than models trained with the true bound, even though the samples look better. Nichol and Dhariwal (2021) recover good likelihoods by also learning the variances Σθ\Sigma_\thetaΣθ​ and adding a small weight on the true bound ("hybrid loss"); Kingma et al. (2021, Variational Diffusion Models) learn the schedule and optimize the bound directly.

The training algorithm is therefore four lines: sample a data point, a random step ttt and noise ϵ\epsilonϵ; build xtx_txt​ with the closed form; predict the noise; take a gradient step on the squared error. Sampling (Ho et al., Algorithm 2) starts from xT∼N(0,I)x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)xT​∼N(0,I) and for t=T,…,1t=T,\dots,1t=T,…,1 draws

xt−1=1αt(xt−βt1−αˉt ϵθ(xt,t))+σtz,z∼N(0,I)  (z=0 at t=1).x_{t-1}=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\Big)+\sigma_t z,\qquad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\ \ (z=0\text{ at }t=1).xt−1​=αt​​1​(xt​−1−αˉt​​βt​​ϵθ​(xt​,t))+σt​z,z∼N(0,I)  (z=0 at t=1).

This is the ancestral sampler: a learned deterministic drift followed by injected noise. It needs TTT sequential network evaluations (1000 in the original), the main cost of diffusion.

Parameterizations: epsilon, x0, and v

Because xt=αˉtx0+1−αˉtϵx_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilonxt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ is one linear equation in two unknowns, predicting ϵ\epsilonϵ is equivalent to predicting x0x_0x0​ given xtx_txt​ and ttt:

x^0=xt−1−αˉt ϵ^αˉt.\hat x_0=\frac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat\epsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}} .x^0​=αˉt​​xt​−1−αˉt​​ϵ^​.

So there are several "equivalent" prediction targets, and they differ only in the implicit loss weighting and in numerical conditioning:

Target Network output Best when Weakness
ϵ\epsilonϵ the added noise moderate to low noise; the DDPM default At t→Tt\to Tt→T, x^0\hat x_0x^0​ divides by αˉt≈0\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\approx0αˉt​​≈0, amplifying errors
x0x_0x0​ the clean data very high noise Blurry predictions at low noise; weak signal for fine detail
vvv v=αˉt ϵ−1−αˉt x0v=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0v=αˉt​​ϵ−1−αˉt​​x0​ all noise levels; few-step distillation Slightly less intuitive

v-prediction (Salimans and Ho, 2022, in the progressive-distillation paper) is a rotation. In the (x0,ϵ)(x_0,\epsilon)(x0​,ϵ) plane, xtx_txt​ is a point on a circle of "angle" ϕt\phi_tϕt​ with cos⁡ϕt=αˉt\cos\phi_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}cosϕt​=αˉt​​, sin⁡ϕt=1−αˉt\sin\phi_t=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}sinϕt​=1−αˉt​​, and vvv is the velocity of xtx_txt​ as ϕ\phiϕ increases (v=∂xt/∂ϕv=\partial x_t/\partial\phiv=∂xt​/∂ϕ). You can recover both ingredients by rotating back:

x^0=αˉt xt−1−αˉt v^,ϵ^=1−αˉt xt+αˉt v^.\hat x_0=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat v,\qquad \hat\epsilon=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t+\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat v .x^0​=αˉt​​xt​−1−αˉt​​v^,ϵ^=1−αˉt​​xt​+αˉt​​v^.

(Check the first: αˉxt−1−αˉ v=αˉx0+αˉ(1−αˉ)ϵ−αˉ(1−αˉ)ϵ+(1−αˉ)x0=x0\sqrt{\bar\alpha}x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha}\,v=\bar\alpha x_0+\sqrt{\bar\alpha(1-\bar\alpha)}\epsilon-\sqrt{\bar\alpha(1-\bar\alpha)}\epsilon+(1-\bar\alpha)x_0=x_0αˉ​xt​−1−αˉ​v=αˉx0​+αˉ(1−αˉ)​ϵ−αˉ(1−αˉ)​ϵ+(1−αˉ)x0​=x0​.) Its main virtue is that the target stays well scaled (unit variance) at both ends of the schedule, whereas ϵ\epsilonϵ-prediction becomes ill-conditioned at the nearly-pure-noise end. The next code block implements the conversions.

pythonparameterizations.py
import torch

def to_x0(x_t, out, ab, kind):
    """Convert a network output to an x0 estimate. ab = alpha_bar_t, broadcastable to x_t."""
    if kind == "eps":
        return (x_t - (1 - ab).sqrt() * out) / ab.sqrt()
    if kind == "x0":
        return out
    if kind == "v":
        return ab.sqrt() * x_t - (1 - ab).sqrt() * out
    raise ValueError(kind)

def to_eps(x_t, out, ab, kind):
    if kind == "eps":
        return out
    if kind == "x0":                                  # solve x_t = sqrt(ab) x0 + sqrt(1-ab) eps for eps
        return (x_t - ab.sqrt() * out) / (1 - ab).sqrt()
    if kind == "v":
        return (1 - ab).sqrt() * x_t + ab.sqrt() * out
    raise ValueError(kind)

def training_target(x0, eps, ab, kind):
    return {"eps": eps, "x0": x0, "v": ab.sqrt() * eps - (1 - ab).sqrt() * x0}[kind]

# self-test: all conversions must be mutually consistent
torch.manual_seed(0)
x0, eps = torch.randn(4, 3, 8, 8), torch.randn(4, 3, 8, 8)
ab = torch.tensor([0.9, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01]).view(-1, 1, 1, 1)
x_t = ab.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - ab).sqrt() * eps
for kind in ["eps", "x0", "v"]:
    out = training_target(x0, eps, ab, kind)
    print(kind, (to_x0(x_t, out, ab, kind) - x0).abs().max().item(), (to_eps(x_t, out, ab, kind) - eps).abs().max().item())

Loss weighting and the SNR

Everything above can be restated as "what weight does each noise level get in the x0x_0x0​-reconstruction error?". Using ϵ^−ϵ=SNR (x0−x^0)\hat\epsilon-\epsilon=\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}}\,(x_0-\hat x_0)ϵ^−ϵ=SNR​(x0​−x^0​) (this follows from holding xtx_txt​ fixed in the closed form), we get:

∥ϵ−ϵ^∥2=SNR(t) ∥x0−x^0∥2,∥v−v^∥2=(1+SNR(t)) ∥x0−x^0∥2.\|\epsilon-\hat\epsilon\|^2=\mathrm{SNR}(t)\,\|x_0-\hat x_0\|^2,\qquad \|v-\hat v\|^2=\big(1+\mathrm{SNR}(t)\big)\,\|x_0-\hat x_0\|^2 .∥ϵ−ϵ^∥2=SNR(t)∥x0​−x^0​∥2,∥v−v^∥2=(1+SNR(t))∥x0​−x^0​∥2.

So the ϵ\epsilonϵ-loss is a SNR-weighted x0x_0x0​-loss, and the vvv-loss is the same plus a constant, which keeps a nonvanishing weight at high noise. The chart shows the weights.

Noise schedules

The schedule decides how the finite budget of TTT steps is spent across noise levels. Two schedules dominate the literature.

Linear (Ho et al., 2020): βt\beta_tβt​ increases linearly from 10−410^{-4}10−4 to 0.020.020.02 with T=1000T=1000T=1000. This was tuned for 32×3232\times3232×32 images.

Cosine (Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021): define αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​ directly, αˉt=f(t)f(0),f(t)=cos⁡2 ⁣(t/T+s1+s⋅π2),s=0.008,\bar\alpha_t=\frac{f(t)}{f(0)},\qquad f(t)=\cos^2\!\Big(\frac{t/T+s}{1+s}\cdot\frac\pi2\Big),\quad s=0.008,αˉt​=f(0)f(t)​,f(t)=cos2(1+st/T+s​⋅2π​),s=0.008, and clip each implied βt=1−αˉt/αˉt−1\beta_t=1-\bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_{t-1}βt​=1−αˉt​/αˉt−1​ to at most 0.9990.9990.999 to avoid singularities near t=Tt=Tt=T. The offset sss keeps βt\beta_tβt​ from being too tiny at the start.

A cleaner way to compare schedules is the log-SNR λt=log⁡αˉt1−αˉt\lambda_t=\log\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}λt​=log1−αˉt​αˉt​​. Any schedule is a monotone curve λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t); what the model sees at a given noise level does not depend on ttt itself, only on λ\lambdaλ. Equal spacing in ttt translates into a particular density of training samples along the λ\lambdaλ axis.

Practical consequences:

  • Resolution matters. At higher resolution neighboring pixels are redundant, so the same noise variance destroys less information; high-resolution models need a schedule shifted toward more noise (a lower SNR at every ttt). Hoogeboom et al. (2023, "simple diffusion") and Stable Diffusion 3 both rescale the schedule with image size. Treat a schedule tuned for 32x32 as a starting point, not a law.
  • Zero terminal SNR. Both schedules leave a small leftover signal at t=Tt=Tt=T (αˉT>0\bar\alpha_T>0αˉT​>0; for the cosine schedule it is clipped to avoid exactly zero). At sampling time the model is then started from pure noise that does not match what it saw at t=Tt=Tt=T, which can cause a bias toward medium brightness in generated images. Lin et al. (2024) analyze this and recommend enforcing αˉT=0\bar\alpha_T=0αˉT​=0 together with vvv-prediction.
  • Schedules are part of the model. Changing the schedule at sampling time without retraining is possible only through careful re-timing (see Karras et al. below), because the network was trained for a specific mapping from ttt to noise level.
  • Karras et al. (2022, "EDM") argue for abandoning discrete steps and designing the noise level σ\sigmaσ, the loss weighting, the network preconditioning and the sampler separately; their recipe is a good example of how much of "diffusion quality" is in these design choices rather than in the core idea.

Score matching and the denoising view

The score function

The score of a density ppp is the gradient of its log-density with respect to the data, not the parameters: s(x)=∇xlog⁡p(x).s(x)=\nabla_x\log p(x).s(x)=∇x​logp(x). It is a vector field that points uphill on the log-density landscape; for a Gaussian N(μ,σ2I)\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2I)N(μ,σ2I) it is −(x−μ)/σ2-(x-\mu)/\sigma^2−(x−μ)/σ2, an arrow toward the mean whose length grows with distance. Two properties make scores attractive for generative modeling. First, the score does not depend on the normalizing constant: ∇xlog⁡(p~(x)/Z)=∇xlog⁡p~(x)\nabla_x\log\big(\tilde p(x)/Z\big)=\nabla_x\log\tilde p(x)∇x​log(p~​(x)/Z)=∇x​logp~​(x), so you can model an unnormalized density without computing ZZZ. Second, given a score you can sample by following it with noise (Langevin dynamics): xk+1=xk+η2 ∇xlog⁡p(xk)+η zk,zk∼N(0,I),x_{k+1}=x_k+\tfrac{\eta}{2}\,\nabla_x\log p(x_k)+\sqrt{\eta}\,z_k,\qquad z_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I),xk+1​=xk​+2η​∇x​logp(xk​)+η​zk​,zk​∼N(0,I), which under mild conditions converges to samples from ppp as η→0\eta\to0η→0 and k→∞k\to\inftyk→∞.

Why one noise level is not enough

Estimating ∇xlog⁡pdata\nabla_x\log p_\text{data}∇x​logpdata​ directly has two problems on real data. The data lie near a low-dimensional manifold, so the density is essentially zero (and its score undefined) off the manifold; and in the low-density regions between modes there are almost no training samples, so the score estimate there is poor, and that is exactly where Langevin chains start. Song and Ermon (2019) fixed both by perturbing the data with Gaussian noise at many scales σ1>σ2>⋯>σL\sigma_1>\sigma_2>\dots>\sigma_Lσ1​>σ2​>⋯>σL​ and learning one network conditioned on the noise level. Heavy noise fills space with probability mass and gives the network a signal everywhere; light noise restores the fine structure. Sampling then goes from the largest to the smallest noise level (annealed Langevin dynamics). This is already the structure of diffusion.

Denoising score matching

We cannot regress on ∇log⁡pσ(x)\nabla\log p_\sigma(x)∇logpσ​(x) directly because we do not know it. Vincent (2011) showed that for a Gaussian corruption kernel the unknown quantity can be replaced by a known one.

Let x~=x+σϵ\tilde x=x+\sigma\epsilonx~=x+σϵ with x∼pdatax\sim p_\text{data}x∼pdata​, ϵ∼N(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)ϵ∼N(0,I), and pσ(x~)=∫pdata(x) qσ(x~∣x) dxp_\sigma(\tilde x)=\int p_\text{data}(x)\,q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)\,dxpσ​(x~)=∫pdata​(x)qσ​(x~∣x)dx. The explicit score matching loss would be JESM(θ)=12Ex~∼pσ∥sθ(x~)−∇x~log⁡pσ(x~)∥2,J_\text{ESM}(\theta)=\tfrac12\E_{\tilde x\sim p_\sigma}\big\|s_\theta(\tilde x)-\nabla_{\tilde x}\log p_\sigma(\tilde x)\big\|^2,JESM​(θ)=21​Ex~∼pσ​​​sθ​(x~)−∇x~​logpσ​(x~)​2, whose target is unknown. The denoising version uses the known conditional score ∇x~log⁡qσ(x~∣x)=−(x~−x)/σ2=−ϵ/σ\nabla_{\tilde x}\log q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)=-(\tilde x-x)/\sigma^2=-\epsilon/\sigma∇x~​logqσ​(x~∣x)=−(x~−x)/σ2=−ϵ/σ: JDSM(θ)=12Ex,x~∥sθ(x~)−∇x~log⁡qσ(x~∣x)∥2.J_\text{DSM}(\theta)=\tfrac12\E_{x,\tilde x}\big\|s_\theta(\tilde x)-\nabla_{\tilde x}\log q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)\big\|^2 .JDSM​(θ)=21​Ex,x~​​sθ​(x~)−∇x~​logqσ​(x~∣x)​2.
