Epsilon-prediction is score estimation

Now apply DSM to the diffusion kernel q(xt∣x0)=N(αˉtx0,(1−αˉt)I)q(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I)q(xt​∣x0​)=N(αˉt​​x0​,(1−αˉt​)I). Its conditional score is ∇xtlog⁡q(xt∣x0)=−xt−αˉtx01−αˉt=−ϵ1−αˉt.\nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0)=-\frac{x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0}{1-\bar\alpha_t}=-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}} .∇xt​​logq(xt​∣x0​)=−1−αˉt​xt​−αˉt​​x0​​=−1−αˉt​​ϵ​. So training a network sθ(xt,t)s_\theta(x_t,t)sθ​(xt​,t) by DSM is the same as training ϵθ\epsilon_\thetaϵθ​ by Lsimple\mathcal L_\text{simple}Lsimple​, with  sθ(xt,t)=−ϵθ(xt,t)1−αˉt .\boxed{\ s_\theta(x_t,t)=-\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\ }. sθ​(xt​,t)=−1−αˉt​​ϵθ​(xt​,t)​ ​. In words: the noise that was added points away from the data; the score points toward it. The DDPM denoiser is a score estimator at every noise level, and the weights of the simplified loss correspond to the DSM weighting λ(σ)∝σ2\lambda(\sigma)\propto\sigma^2λ(σ)∝σ2 used by Song and Ermon. There is also a neat identity named after Tweedie (and Robbins): the posterior mean of the clean data given the noisy point is E[x0∣xt]=xt+(1−αˉt) ∇xtlog⁡pt(xt)αˉt,\E[x_0\mid x_t]=\frac{x_t+(1-\bar\alpha_t)\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p_t(x_t)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}},E[x0​∣xt​]=αˉt​​xt​+(1−αˉt​)∇xt​​logpt​(xt​)​, which is the x^0\hat x_0x^0​ of parameterizations once ϵ^=−1−αˉt s\hat\epsilon=-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,sϵ^=−1−αˉt​​s is substituted. The denoiser is the score, up to an affine change.

What the network actually learns

At noise level σ\sigmaσ the best possible guess of the clean point is the average of all clean points that could have produced xtx_txt​, weighted by how likely each is. At high noise that average is a blurry blob near the data mean; at low noise it snaps to the nearest data point. The score field is "where that average sits, relative to me". Sampling is a long walk guided by this arrow field, starting where the arrows are smooth and global and ending where they are sharp and local.

InteractiveScore field and reverse process on a 2-D Gaussian mixture (exact score)

The SDE view and the probability-flow ODE

The discrete chain with T=1000T=1000T=1000 is a time discretization of a continuous-time process. Song et al. (2021) took the limit T→∞T\to\inftyT→∞.

Forward SDE

A stochastic differential equation describes a process with a drift fff and a noise term driven by Brownian motion WtW_tWt​: dx=f(x,t) dt+g(t) dWt.dx=f(x,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t .dx=f(x,t)dt+g(t)dWt​. The DDPM chain is the Euler-Maruyama discretization of the variance-preserving (VP) SDE dx=−12β(t) x dt+β(t) dWt,dx=-\tfrac12\beta(t)\,x\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t,dx=−21​β(t)xdt+β(t)​dWt​, where β(t)\beta(t)β(t) is the continuous-time analogue of βt\beta_tβt​ (so βt≈β(t)Δt\beta_t\approx\beta(t)\Delta tβt​≈β(t)Δt). Its marginals are exactly the Gaussian form we derived, xt=αˉ(t)x0+1−αˉ(t)ϵx_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha(t)}\epsilonxt​=αˉ(t)​x0​+1−αˉ(t)​ϵ with αˉ(t)=exp⁡(−∫0tβ(s) ds)\bar\alpha(t)=\exp(-\int_0^t\beta(s)\,ds)αˉ(t)=exp(−∫0t​β(s)ds). The older score-network line (NCSN) corresponds to the variance-exploding (VE) SDE dx=dσ2(t)/dt dWtdx=\sqrt{d\sigma^2(t)/dt}\,dW_tdx=dσ2(t)/dt​dWt​, with no shrinking drift and noise that grows without bound.

Reverse-time SDE

A theorem of Anderson (1982) says that the time-reversal of this process is again a diffusion, with the same noise scale but a drift corrected by the score: dx=[f(x,t)−g(t)2 ∇xlog⁡pt(x)]dt+g(t) dWˉt,dx=\Big[f(x,t)-g(t)^2\,\nabla_x\log p_t(x)\Big]dt+g(t)\,d\bar W_t,dx=[f(x,t)−g(t)2∇x​logpt​(x)]dt+g(t)dWˉt​, where time runs backward from TTT to 000 and Wˉ\bar WWˉ is a Brownian motion in reverse time. This is the entire mathematical content of diffusion sampling: knowing the score of every marginal ptp_tpt​ gives you a generative process. A network trained by denoising score matching supplies sθ≈∇log⁡pts_\theta\approx\nabla\log p_tsθ​≈∇logpt​, and any SDE solver produces samples. The DDPM ancestral sampler is one particular discretization of the reverse VP-SDE.

The probability-flow ODE

Remarkably, the same family of marginals {pt}\{p_t\}{pt​} is produced by a deterministic process: dxdt=f(x,t)−12 g(t)2 ∇xlog⁡pt(x).\frac{dx}{dt}=f(x,t)-\tfrac12\,g(t)^2\,\nabla_x\log p_t(x).dtdx​=f(x,t)−21​g(t)2∇x​logpt​(x). The reason, in one line, is that the Fokker-Planck equation (which governs how the density ptp_tpt​ evolves) only depends on the combination of drift and diffusion, and the term 12g2∇log⁡pt\tfrac12g^2\nabla\log p_t21​g2∇logpt​ can be moved between the "drift" and "diffusion" columns without changing ptp_tpt​. The ODE has no randomness, so:

  • Each noise sample xTx_TxT​ maps to exactly one image x0x_0x0​ (a smooth, invertible map): you can encode an image to noise by integrating forward. This gives meaningful latent interpolation and image editing (SDEdit, inversion).
  • You can use fast, high-order ODE solvers (Runge-Kutta, multistep) instead of 1000 stochastic steps. This is the theoretical foundation for DDIM, DPM-Solver and the EDM samplers.
  • With a neural score you can compute exact likelihoods via the instantaneous change-of-variables formula, as in continuous normalizing flows (see flows).
Stochastic versus deterministic samplers

Both families target the same marginals when the score is exact, but they behave differently with an imperfect network. Stochastic samplers can correct earlier errors (each step re-randomizes) and often give slightly better quality at many steps; deterministic ODE samplers are much more efficient at few steps and give a one-to-one noise-to-image map. In practice you will see both: ancestral samplers for quality at 50-250 steps, deterministic solvers for 10-30 steps.

DDIM and fast sampling

Sampling with 1000 sequential network calls is the practical bottleneck: an image takes seconds to minutes. Song, Meng and Ermon (2021, DDIM, "Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models") observed that the DDPM training objective depends only on the marginals q(xt∣x0)q(x_t\mid x_0)q(xt​∣x0​), not on the joint Markov structure. Therefore many different (non-Markovian) forward processes share the same marginals and the same trained network, and some of them admit deterministic, much shorter reverse chains.

The DDIM update

Given the network output at a step ttt, form the clean estimate x^0=(xt−1−αˉt ϵθ)/αˉt\hat x_0=(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x^0​=(xt​−1−αˉt​​ϵθ​)/αˉt​​. For any earlier step s<ts<ts<t (not necessarily t−1t-1t−1) the DDIM update is xs=αˉs x^0+1−αˉs−σ2 ϵθ(xt,t)+σ z,σ=η1−αˉs1−αˉt1−αˉtαˉs,x_s=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_s}\ \hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_s-\sigma^2}\ \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)+\sigma\,z,\qquad \sigma=\eta\sqrt{\tfrac{1-\bar\alpha_s}{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\sqrt{1-\tfrac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_s}},xs​=αˉs​​ x^0​+1−αˉs​−σ2​ ϵθ​(xt​,t)+σz,σ=η1−αˉt​1−αˉs​​​1−αˉs​αˉt​​​, with z∼N(0,I)z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)z∼N(0,I). Read it as: go to the predicted clean image, then re-noise it to level sss using a mix of the predicted noise direction and fresh noise.

  • η=1\eta=1η=1 recovers DDPM ancestral sampling (when s=t−1s=t-1s=t−1).
  • η=0\eta=0η=0 gives σ=0\sigma=0σ=0: a deterministic map, an Euler discretization of the probability-flow ODE written in the variable x/αˉx/\sqrt{\bar\alpha}x/αˉ​ versus (1−αˉ)/αˉ\sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha)/\bar\alpha}(1−αˉ)/αˉ​.
  • Any decreasing subsequence T=τS>⋯>τ0=0T=\tau_S>\dots>\tau_0=0T=τS​>⋯>τ0​=0 can be used: S=20S=20S=20 or 505050 network evaluations instead of 1000.

The code below implements both samplers for a one-dimensional two-Gaussian mixture where the optimal noise predictor is known in closed form, so any error you see comes from the sampler, not from a learned network. It produces the numbers in the next chart.

pythonddim_toy_exact_score.py
import numpy as np

# Data: 1-D mixture 0.5 N(-2, 0.5^2) + 0.5 N(+2, 0.5^2).  Linear schedule, T = 1000.
T = 1000
betas = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)
ab = np.concatenate([[1.0], np.cumprod(1 - betas)])          # ab[k] = alpha_bar at step k, ab[0] = 1
mus, sg, wts = np.array([-2.0, 2.0]), 0.5, np.array([0.5, 0.5])

def eps_star(x, k):
    """Exact optimal noise predictor E[eps | x_t] = -sqrt(1-ab) * score_k(x)."""
    a = ab[k]
    m = np.sqrt(a) * mus[None, :]                              # component means at noise level k
    v = a * sg**2 + 1 - a                                      # component variance at noise level k
    logp = np.log(wts)[None, :] - 0.5 * (x[:, None] - m) ** 2 / v - 0.5 * np.log(v)
    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)   # responsibilities
    score = -(p * (x[:, None] - m) / v).sum(1)
    return -np.sqrt(1 - a) * score

def sample(n_steps, eta, N=20000, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ks = np.round(np.linspace(T, 0, n_steps + 1)).astype(int)   # decreasing time grid
    x = rng.standard_normal(N)
    for t, s in zip(ks[:-1], ks[1:]):
        e = eps_star(x, t)
        x0 = (x - np.sqrt(1 - ab[t]) * e) / np.sqrt(ab[t])
        sig = eta * np.sqrt((1 - ab[s]) / (1 - ab[t])) * np.sqrt(1 - ab[t] / ab[s])
        x = np.sqrt(ab[s]) * x0 + np.sqrt(max(1 - ab[s] - sig**2, 0)) * e + sig * rng.standard_normal(N)
    return x

def w1_to_truth(x, rng=np.random.default_rng(0)):
    ref = np.sort(np.concatenate([rng.normal(-2, .5, 200000), rng.normal(2, .5, 200000)]))
    q = np.quantile(ref, np.linspace(0, 1, len(x) + 2)[1:-1])
    return np.abs(np.sort(x) - q).mean()                         # 1-D Wasserstein-1 distance

for n in [5, 20, 100, 1000]:
    print(n, "DDIM", round(w1_to_truth(sample(n, 0.0)), 4), "DDPM", round(w1_to_truth(sample(n, 1.0)), 4))

The chart shows the main trend of the field: a 20-50 step deterministic sampler already reaches an error within a factor of a few of the 1000-step floor. In real image models the picture is similar, and later solvers (DPM-Solver, Lu et al. 2022; the EDM Heun sampler, Karras et al. 2022; UniPC) push good samples down to 10-20 evaluations by using higher-order ODE solvers, because the probability-flow trajectory is smooth.

Beyond solvers: distillation

Solver improvements reduce the number of steps to roughly 10-20. To go lower, you change the model. Progressive distillation (Salimans and Ho, 2022) trains a student to match two teacher steps with one, halving the step count repeatedly (8, 4, 2 steps). Consistency models (Song et al., 2023) train a network that maps any point on a probability-flow trajectory to the trajectory's endpoint, enabling one- or two-step generation. Adversarial distillation variants (for example, SDXL-Turbo, 2023) add a GAN loss to the few-step student. Distilled models trade some diversity and flexibility (for instance, worse behavior under strong guidance) for speed. The distinction to remember: solvers change how a fixed network is used; distillation changes the network.

Flow matching and rectified flows

A closely related recipe, flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) and rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023), trains a network to predict a velocity field along a straight-line interpolation xt=(1−t) x0+t ϵx_t=(1-t)\,x_0+t\,\epsilonxt​=(1−t)x0​+tϵ between data and noise, with the regression target ϵ−x0\epsilon-x_0ϵ−x0​. Sampling integrates an ODE; no SDE or variance schedule is needed. It is a vvv-prediction-like objective with a different path, and it underlies several recent large models (for instance Stable Diffusion 3 uses a rectified-flow formulation). Everything in this week transfers: only the interpolation path and the time parameterization change.

Diffusion as a hierarchical VAE

The ELBO we derived above is formally the ELBO of a Markovian hierarchical VAE: the latents are zt=xtz_t=x_tzt​=xt​, the encoder q(x1:T∣x0)q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)q(x1:T​∣x0​) is the forward process, the decoder chain is pθ(xt−1∣xt)p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)pθ​(xt−1​∣xt​). Comparing with Week 12:

Standard VAE Diffusion model
Latent dimension much smaller than the data the same as the data, TTT copies
Encoder learned qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z\mid x)qϕ​(z∣x) fixed, Gaussian noising, no parameters
Decoder one network call TTT network calls, each a small denoising step
Posterior collapse a real risk impossible: the latents are fixed noisy copies of the input
KL term per-sample KL to the prior, trades off with reconstruction sum of TTT KLs between Gaussians, each a denoising regression
Blurriness mean-prediction of one big step is blurry each step is tiny, so predicting the mean is accurate

This explains why diffusion succeeds where a one-step Gaussian decoder fails. The blurriness of a VAE comes from asking a unimodal Gaussian decoder to capture a multimodal p(x∣z)p(x\mid z)p(x∣z). In diffusion each step really is nearly Gaussian (a small perturbation of xtx_txt​), so the Gaussian assumption is nearly true, and multimodality is resolved gradually across steps. It also explains why the objective is stable: with the encoder frozen, there is no adversary and no joint optimization of encoder and decoder. The cost is sampling speed: instead of one decoder pass you need many. A recurring theme is to combine the two: a VAE compresses images into a short, perceptually meaningful code, and diffusion models that code, which is exactly latent diffusion (below).

Conditioning and guidance

An unconditional sampler is a curiosity; useful systems let you say what to generate: a class label, a text prompt, a sketch, a low-resolution image. Mathematically we want p(x∣c)p(x\mid c)p(x∣c). The score decomposes by Bayes' rule:

∇xtlog⁡pt(xt∣c)=∇xtlog⁡pt(xt)+∇xtlog⁡pt(c∣xt).\nabla_{x_t}\log p_t(x_t\mid c)=\nabla_{x_t}\log p_t(x_t)+\nabla_{x_t}\log p_t(c\mid x_t).∇xt​​logpt​(xt​∣c)=∇xt​​logpt​(xt​)+∇xt​​logpt​(c∣xt​).

The first term is the unconditional score we already have; the second pushes the sample toward regions where the condition ccc is likely.

Classifier guidance

Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) trained a separate noisy-image classifier pϕ(c∣xt)p_\phi(c\mid x_t)pϕ​(c∣xt​) (a classifier trained on images corrupted at every noise level) and added its gradient to the sampler, scaled by a guidance scale www: s~(xt,c)=∇log⁡p(xt)+w ∇xtlog⁡pϕ(c∣xt)⟺ϵ~=ϵθ(xt,t)−w1−αˉt ∇xtlog⁡pϕ(c∣xt).\tilde s(x_t,c)=\nabla\log p(x_t)+w\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p_\phi(c\mid x_t) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tilde\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)-w\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p_\phi(c\mid x_t).s~(xt​,c)=∇logp(xt​)+w∇xt​​logpϕ​(c∣xt​)⟺ϵ~=ϵθ​(xt​,t)−w1−αˉt​​∇xt​​logpϕ​(c∣xt​). With w=1w=1w=1 this samples from the true conditional. With w>1w>1w>1 it samples from the sharpened distribution p(x) p(c∣x)wp(x)\,p(c\mid x)^wp(x)p(c∣x)w, which concentrates on points the classifier is very sure about. Their "ADM-G" model, with guidance, outperformed the best GANs of the time on ImageNet (FID), the paper's title ("Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis") being a landmark. The cost: you need to train and run a second network on noisy images, the classifier gradient can be adversarial (the sample may fool the classifier rather than look like class ccc), and it only works for conditions you can classify.

Classifier-free guidance

Ho and Salimans (2022) removed the classifier. The trick is to train one network on both the conditional and the unconditional task by randomly replacing the condition with a null token ∅\varnothing∅ (typically 10-20% of the time), so that ϵθ(xt,t,c)\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c)ϵθ​(xt​,t,c) and ϵθ(xt,t,∅)\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,\varnothing)ϵθ​(xt​,t,∅) are two heads of one set of weights. Then the classifier gradient is implicit.

Derivation: classifier-free guidance

Rearrange Bayes' rule for the score: ∇log⁡p(c∣xt)=∇log⁡p(xt∣c)−∇log⁡p(xt)\nabla\log p(c\mid x_t)=\nabla\log p(x_t\mid c)-\nabla\log p(x_t)∇logp(c∣xt​)=∇logp(xt​∣c)−∇logp(xt​). Using ϵ=−1−αˉt s\epsilon=-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,sϵ=−1−αˉt​​s, with ϵc=ϵθ(xt,t,c)\epsilon_c=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c)ϵc​=ϵθ​(xt​,t,c) and ϵ∅=ϵθ(xt,t,∅)\epsilon_\varnothing=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,\varnothing)ϵ∅​=ϵθ​(xt​,t,∅), ∇log⁡p(c∣xt) ≈ −11−αˉt(ϵc−ϵ∅).\nabla\log p(c\mid x_t)\ \approx\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\big(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_\varnothing\big).∇logp(c∣xt​) ≈ −1−αˉt​​1​(ϵc​−ϵ∅​). Plug into the classifier-guided score ∇log⁡p(xt)+w ∇log⁡p(c∣xt)\nabla\log p(x_t)+w\,\nabla\log p(c\mid x_t)∇logp(xt​)+w∇logp(c∣xt​) and convert back to a noise prediction:  ϵ~=ϵ∅+w (ϵc−ϵ∅)=(1−w) ϵ∅+w ϵc \boxed{\ \tilde\epsilon=\epsilon_\varnothing+w\,\big(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_\varnothing\big)=(1-w)\,\epsilon_\varnothing+w\,\epsilon_c\ } ϵ~=ϵ∅​+w(ϵc​−ϵ∅​)=(1−w)ϵ∅​+wϵc​ ​ The effective density being sampled is p~(x∣c)∝p(x∣c) w p(x) 1−w∝p(x) p(c∣x)w\tilde p(x\mid c)\propto p(x\mid c)^{\,w}\,p(x)^{\,1-w}\propto p(x)\,p(c\mid x)^{w}p~​(x∣c)∝p(x∣c)wp(x)1−w∝p(x)p(c∣x)w.

Convention warning. Ho and Salimans write the guided prediction as (1+w) ϵc−w ϵ∅(1+w)\,\epsilon_c-w\,\epsilon_\varnothing(1+w)ϵc​−wϵ∅​, so their w=0w=0w=0 is the plain conditional model. The formula above uses where=1+wtheirsw_\text{here}=1+w_\text{theirs}where​=1+wtheirs​. Libraries are not consistent either: the "guidance_scale" in Hugging Face diffusers equals wherew_\text{here}where​ (1 means no guidance; typical text-to-image values are 5 to 9). Always check which convention a codebase uses.

What guidance does. The difference ϵc−ϵ∅\epsilon_c-\epsilon_\varnothingϵc​−ϵ∅​ is "the part of the denoising direction that is due to the condition". Multiplying it by w>1w>1w>1 exaggerates the prompt. The effect is not just sharper images but a distribution change: samples move toward high-likelihood, prototypical examples of the class, away from the boundary with other classes. You get higher fidelity and prompt adherence at the price of diversity and, at very high www, over-saturated, high-contrast, artifact-prone images. The next demo computes the idealized guided density exactly for two Gaussian classes, and the chart summarizes a sampling experiment.

InteractiveClassifier-free guidance on two Gaussian classes: sharper and less diverse as w grows
The price of high guidance

Because the guided density is not the true conditional, high www gives non-physical samples: with the same www the guided distribution has a different mean and a smaller variance than the data, so metrics like FID typically follow a U-shape (best at moderate www) while Inception Score and CLIP score keep improving. Remedies in the literature include guidance intervals (apply guidance only in the middle of the trajectory), dynamic thresholding (Imagen, Saharia et al. 2022: clip and rescale the predicted x0x_0x0​ to avoid saturation) and rescaling the guided prediction to match the standard deviation of ϵc\epsilon_cϵc​.

The training change is tiny

Classifier-free guidance requires almost no extra code in training: randomly drop the condition. The following fragment shows the two places it touches a codebase (training with dropout, sampling with two passes).

pythoncfg_core.py
import torch

NULL_LABEL = 10                                      # MNIST has classes 0..9; index 10 means "no condition"

def drop_condition(y, p_uncond=0.1):
    """Training: replace labels with the null token with probability p_uncond."""
    mask = torch.rand(y.shape[0], device=y.device) < p_uncond
    return torch.where(mask, torch.full_like(y, NULL_LABEL), y)

@torch.no_grad()
def guided_eps(model, x_t, t, y, w):
    """Sampling: two passes of the same network, then extrapolate (w = 1: plain conditional model)."""
    if w == 1.0:
        return model(x_t, t, y)
    # batch the two passes together for efficiency
    x2, t2 = torch.cat([x_t, x_t]), torch.cat([t, t])
    y2 = torch.cat([y, torch.full_like(y, NULL_LABEL)])
    eps_c, eps_u = model(x2, t2, y2).chunk(2)
    return eps_u + w * (eps_c - eps_u)

Text-to-image conditioning with cross-attention

For text, the condition is a sequence of token embeddings, not a single label. Systems encode the prompt with a frozen language model (CLIP's text encoder in Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x, Week 11; T5 in Imagen; combinations in later systems) into a matrix C∈RL×dcC\in\R^{L\times d_c}C∈RL×dc​ (for example L=77L=77L=77 tokens). The denoiser injects it through cross-attention layers (Week 9): the queries come from the image features, the keys and values from the text tokens, CrossAttn(F,C)=softmax⁡ ⁣((FWQ)(CWK)⊤d) (CWV),\mathrm{CrossAttn}(F,C)=\softmax\!\Big(\frac{(FW_Q)(CW_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)\,(CW_V),CrossAttn(F,C)=softmax(d​(FWQ​)(CWK​)⊤​)(CWV​), with F∈RN×dfF\in\R^{N\times d_f}F∈RN×df​ the NNN spatial positions of a feature map. Each spatial position decides which words to read from, and the attention maps are interpretable: the map for the word "dog" highlights where the dog is (the basis of prompt-to-prompt editing). Timestep information is injected separately (see the architecture section). Classifier-free guidance is used for text exactly as above, with the empty prompt as the null condition; negative prompts simply replace ϵ∅\epsilon_\varnothingϵ∅​ by the prediction for the negative text, so that the extrapolation moves away from the undesired concept.

pythoncross_attention.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class CrossAttention(nn.Module):
    """Image tokens (queries) attend to text tokens (keys/values).
    x: (B, N, d_model)  image features, N = H*W positions
    ctx: (B, L, d_ctx)  text token embeddings, L tokens
    """
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ctx, n_heads=8):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.h, self.dh = n_heads, d_model // n_heads
        self.q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.k = nn.Linear(d_ctx, d_model, bias=False)
        self.v = nn.Linear(d_ctx, d_model, bias=False)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)

    def forward(self, x, ctx, ctx_mask=None):
        B, N, _ = x.shape
        L = ctx.shape[1]
        q = self.q(x).view(B, N, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)    # (B, h, N, dh)
        k = self.k(ctx).view(B, L, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)  # (B, h, L, dh)
        v = self.v(ctx).view(B, L, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)  # (B, h, L, dh)
        attn_mask = None if ctx_mask is None else ctx_mask[:, None, None, :]   # True = keep
        o = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=attn_mask)       # softmax(qk^T/sqrt(dh)) v
        o = o.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, N, -1)
        return self.out(o)

x = torch.randn(2, 32 * 32, 320)       # a 32x32 feature map with 320 channels, flattened
ctx = torch.randn(2, 77, 768)          # 77 text tokens from a 768-d text encoder
print(CrossAttention(320, 768)(x, ctx).shape)    # torch.Size([2, 1024, 320])

Other conditioning mechanisms are variations on the theme: concatenating a low-resolution or masked image to the input channels (super-resolution, inpainting); adaLN/FiLM modulation of normalization layers by a global embedding (class labels, timestep; see DiT below); and adapters such as ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023), which add a trainable copy of the encoder that injects spatial controls (edges, depth, pose) into a frozen model, and LoRA (Week 10) fine-tuning for subjects and styles.

Latent diffusion

Running a denoiser at full pixel resolution is expensive: a 512×512×3512\times512\times3512×512×3 image has 786,432 values and the network must be evaluated dozens of times. Rombach et al. (2022, Latent Diffusion Models, the basis of Stable Diffusion) observed that most pixel bits encode imperceptible high-frequency detail. Their recipe has two stages:

  1. Perceptual compression. Train an autoencoder (a VAE with a small KL penalty and/or a VQ layer, plus an LPIPS perceptual loss and a patch GAN loss; see Week 12) that maps an image x∈R3×512×512x\in\R^{3\times512\times512}x∈R3×512×512 to a latent z=E(x)∈R4×64×64z=E(x)\in\R^{4\times64\times64}z=E(x)∈R4×64×64 with spatial downsampling factor f=8f=8f=8 and decodes it back with DDD.
  2. Latent diffusion. Train the diffusion model on zzz instead of xxx (the loss is the same Lsimple\mathcal L_\text{simple}Lsimple​, with z0=E(x0)z_0=E(x_0)z0​=E(x0​)). Generation: sample zTz_TzT​, denoise to z0z_0z0​, decode x=D(z0)x=D(z_0)x=D(z0​).

The saving is large: 3⋅512⋅512=786,4323\cdot512\cdot512=786{,}4323⋅512⋅512=786,432 pixel values versus 4⋅64⋅64=16,3844\cdot64\cdot64=16{,}3844⋅64⋅64=16,384 latent values, a 48×48\times48× reduction, and self-attention cost (quadratic in positions) falls by a factor of 642=409664^2=4096642=4096 between 5122512^25122 pixel positions and 64264^2642 latent positions. The autoencoder is trained once and reused. Two caveats: the autoencoder's reconstruction ceiling caps the quality (small text and fine facial detail are often lost; newer systems use 16-channel latents), and the latent scale must be normalized to roughly unit variance (Stable Diffusion multiplies latents by a fixed constant, 0.18215 for version 1) so that the noise schedule is meaningful.

Why not just make the VAE strong and skip diffusion?

A VAE's decoder cannot model the global structure of a scene in one Gaussian step (previous section); diffusion handles global structure with a series of small steps. Latent diffusion splits the labor: the autoencoder removes perceptually irrelevant detail, diffusion models the semantic structure that remains. It is the same division of labor as VQ-GAN plus a Transformer prior, with a different prior.

Backbones: U-Net and DiT

The network ϵθ(xt,t,c)\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c)ϵθ​(xt​,t,c) must map a tensor to a tensor of the same shape, using ttt and ccc as side information. Two families are common.

The U-Net

The U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015, for biomedical segmentation) pairs a downsampling path that builds a multi-scale representation with an upsampling path that restores resolution, joined by skip connections that carry fine detail across. Diffusion U-Nets (Ho et al., 2020, building on PixelCNN++ and Wide-ResNet blocks) add:

  • Time conditioning. ttt (or log⁡\loglog-SNR) is mapped through a sinusoidal embedding (as in Transformer positional encodings, Week 9) and an MLP, then added into every residual block (or used for FiLM scale-and-shift).
  • GroupNorm and SiLU activations throughout, rather than BatchNorm, because the per-sample noise level varies and batch statistics would leak across samples.
  • Self-attention at the low-resolution stages (for example 16x16 and 8x8) to capture global structure, and cross-attention blocks for text.
  • Output of the same shape as the input, plus optional variance channels.

U-Nets have a strong inductive bias (locality, multi-scale), are efficient at resolutions up to 64x64 in latent space, and remain the backbone of many deployed systems.

Diffusion Transformers (DiT)

Peebles and Xie (2023, "Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers") replaced the U-Net by a plain Vision Transformer (Week 11) on latent patches. The latent z∈R4×32×32z\in\R^{4\times32\times32}z∈R4×32×32 is cut into p×pp\times pp×p patches (p=2p=2p=2 gives 256 tokens), linearly embedded, and given positional embeddings. The conditioning (timestep and class) is injected by adaptive layer norm: a small MLP maps the conditioning embedding to per-block scales and shifts (γ,β)(\gamma,\beta)(γ,β) and a gate α\alphaα, so that a block computes x←x+α1 Attn(γ1⋅LN(x)+β1)x\leftarrow x+\alpha_1\,\mathrm{Attn}\big(\gamma_1\cdot\mathrm{LN}(x)+\beta_1\big)x←x+α1​Attn(γ1​⋅LN(x)+β1​) and similarly for the MLP. In adaLN-Zero the gates are initialized to zero, so each block is initially the identity, which stabilizes training of deep stacks. The key empirical finding was a clean scaling law: FID improves smoothly as Gflops grow (by more tokens or a larger model), just as for language Transformers (Week 10). Later systems (Stable Diffusion 3, with multimodal Transformer blocks that process text and image tokens jointly, and several video models) use Transformer backbones.

U-Net DiT
Inductive bias convolutional, multi-scale, local none beyond patches and position embeddings
Scaling works, but architecture-specific tuning smooth, predictable scaling in Gflops
Resolution handling fully convolutional, any size needs positional-embedding interpolation
Cost at high resolution cheap in conv layers; attention only at low-res quadratic attention in tokens
Conditioning additive timestep, cross-attention for text adaLN for global, joint or cross attention for text
Reuse of Transformer tooling no yes (FlashAttention, tensor parallelism, etc.)

Neither is "better" in an absolute sense; a Transformer shines when data and compute are plentiful, and the U-Net's bias helps in the small-data regime of your lab. You will build a small U-Net below.

Normalizing flows

Diffusion's probability-flow ODE is one instance of a broader idea: build a generative model by transforming a simple density through an invertible map and track how density changes. This is the normalizing flow family, and unlike VAEs and GANs, flows give the exact log-likelihood.

Change of variables

Let z∼pZz\sim p_Zz∼pZ​ (typically N(0,I)\mathcal N(0,I)N(0,I)) and let x=gθ(z)x=g_\theta(z)x=gθ​(z) with gθg_\thetagθ​ invertible and differentiable, fθ=gθ−1f_\theta=g_\theta^{-1}fθ​=gθ−1​. Then log⁡pX(x)=log⁡pZ(fθ(x))+log⁡∣det⁡∂fθ(x)∂x∣.\log p_X(x)=\log p_Z\big(f_\theta(x)\big)+\log\Big|\det\frac{\partial f_\theta(x)}{\partial x}\Big| .logpX​(x)=logpZ​(fθ​(x))+log​det∂x∂fθ​(x)​​. The derivation is one line from probability conservation, pX(x) ∣dx∣=pZ(z) ∣dz∣p_X(x)\,|dx|=p_Z(z)\,|dz|pX​(x)∣dx∣=pZ​(z)∣dz∣: a map that stretches space must lower the density by the same factor. A deep flow composes KKK maps f=fK∘⋯∘f1f=f_K\circ\dots\circ f_1f=fK​∘⋯∘f1​, and the log-determinants add up. Training maximizes the exact log-likelihood of the data; sampling draws zzz and applies gθ=f1−1∘⋯∘fK−1g_\theta=f_1^{-1}\circ\dots\circ f_K^{-1}gθ​=f1−1​∘⋯∘fK−1​.

For a general D×DD\times DD×D Jacobian the determinant costs O(D3)O(D^3)O(D3) and the inverse is not available, so a flow layer must be designed so that both are cheap. Invertibility plus an easy determinant is the design constraint that limits flows' architectural freedom: you cannot use arbitrary networks or bottlenecks (the dimension must be preserved).

Coupling layers

The influential trick (NICE, Dinh et al. 2015; RealNVP, Dinh et al. 2017) splits x=(xa,xb)x=(x_a,x_b)x=(xa​,xb​) and sets ya=xa,yb=xb⊙exp⁡(s(xa))+t(xa).y_a=x_a,\qquad y_b=x_b\odot\exp\big(s(x_a)\big)+t(x_a).ya​=xa​,yb​=xb​⊙exp(s(xa​))+t(xa​). The functions s,ts,ts,t can be arbitrary neural networks, because they are only ever evaluated in the forward direction. The Jacobian is block-triangular, ∂y∂x=(I0∂yb/∂xadiag(es(xa))),log⁡∣det⁡∂y∂x∣=∑jsj(xa),\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\ \partial y_b/\partial x_a&\mathrm{diag}(e^{s(x_a)})\end{pmatrix},\qquad \log\Big|\det\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\Big|=\sum_j s_j(x_a),∂x∂y​=(I∂yb​/∂xa​​0diag(es(xa​))​),log​det∂x∂y​​=j∑​sj​(xa​), and the inverse is xb=(yb−t(ya))⊙e−s(ya)x_b=(y_b-t(y_a))\odot e^{-s(y_a)}xb​=(yb​−t(ya​))⊙e−s(ya​) with xa=yax_a=y_axa​=ya​. Stacking layers that alternate which half is transformed (checkerboard or channel masks for images) lets every coordinate be transformed. Glow (Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018) added invertible 1×11\times11×1 convolutions and actnorm, and produced high-resolution faces. Here is a compact coupling-layer flow with exact likelihood on a 2-D toy problem.

pythonrealnvp_coupling.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class AffineCoupling(nn.Module):
    """y_a = x_a;  y_b = x_b * exp(s(x_a)) + t(x_a).  `flip` swaps which half is conditioned on."""
    def __init__(self, dim, hidden=128, flip=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.flip, self.d = flip, dim // 2
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(self.d, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, 2 * (dim - self.d)))
        nn.init.zeros_(self.net[-1].weight); nn.init.zeros_(self.net[-1].bias)   # start as the identity map

    def _split(self, x):
        a, b = x[:, :self.d], x[:, self.d:]
        return (b, a) if self.flip else (a, b)

    def forward(self, x):                        # data -> latent, returns (y, log|det J|)
        a, b = self._split(x)
        s, t = self.net(a).chunk(2, dim=1)
        s = torch.tanh(s)                        # bound the log-scale for numerical stability
        y_b = b * torch.exp(s) + t
        y = torch.cat([y_b, a], 1) if self.flip else torch.cat([a, y_b], 1)
        return y, s.sum(1)

    def inverse(self, y):                        # latent -> data
        a, y_b = self._split(y)
        s, t = self.net(a).chunk(2, dim=1)
        s = torch.tanh(s)
        b = (y_b - t) * torch.exp(-s)
        return torch.cat([b, a], 1) if self.flip else torch.cat([a, b], 1)

class Flow(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim=2, n_layers=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([AffineCoupling(dim, flip=(i % 2 == 1)) for i in range(n_layers)])
        self.register_buffer("log_norm", torch.tensor(-0.5 * dim * torch.log(torch.tensor(2 * torch.pi)).item()))

    def log_prob(self, x):
        logdet = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], device=x.device)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x, ld = layer(x); logdet = logdet + ld
        return self.log_norm - 0.5 * (x ** 2).sum(1) + logdet     # log N(z; 0, I) + sum log|det|

    @torch.no_grad()
    def sample(self, n, dim=2):
        z = torch.randn(n, dim, device=self.log_norm.device)
        for layer in reversed(self.layers):
            z = layer.inverse(z)
        return z

flow = Flow()
x = torch.randn(256, 2)
y = x
for l in flow.layers: y, _ = l(y)
for l in reversed(flow.layers): y = l.inverse(y)
print("invertibility error:", (x - y).abs().max().item())      # ~0 (exactly 0 at init)
loss = -flow.log_prob(x).mean()                                 # train with Adam on this NLL
print(loss.item())

The strengths of flows are exact likelihood, a single-pass sampler and a meaningful latent space; the weaknesses are architectural rigidity (full dimension preserved, constrained layers), parameter inefficiency and sample quality that lagged GANs and diffusion. Their mathematical ideas live on: continuous-time flows ("neural ODEs", FFJORD) define the density change through ∂tlog⁡p=−∇⋅v\partial_t\log p=-\nabla\cdot v∂t​logp=−∇⋅v, and the probability-flow ODE of diffusion and the velocity field of flow matching are exactly such continuous flows, trained without needing exact Jacobians.

Autoregressive models

The other exact-likelihood family writes the data distribution as a product of conditionals by the chain rule of probability, pθ(x)=∏i=1Dpθ(xi∣x<i),p_\theta(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{D}p_\theta\big(x_i\mid x_{<i}\big),pθ​(x)=i=1∏D​pθ​(xi​∣x<i​), and trains by maximizing ∑ilog⁡pθ(xi∣x<i)\sum_i\log p_\theta(x_i\mid x_{<i})∑i​logpθ​(xi​∣x<i​), i.e. ordinary cross-entropy (or a mixture likelihood for continuous values), with teacher forcing: all conditionals can be computed in one parallel pass if the architecture enforces causality. Sampling is sequential: draw x1x_1x1​, then x2∣x1x_2\mid x_1x2​∣x1​, and so on. You have already met the dominant instance: the GPT-style language models of Week 10. The question for images and audio is how to impose an ordering and a causal architecture.

PixelRNN and PixelCNN

van den Oord, Kalchbrenner and Kavukcuoglu (2016, PixelRNN/PixelCNN) order pixels in raster scan and model each pixel's three colour channels as a 256-way softmax conditioned on all previous pixels. A masked convolution zeroes the kernel weights that would look at the current pixel (mask type A, first layer) or at future pixels (mask type B, subsequent layers), so a standard convolutional stack computes all conditionals in parallel during training. Later versions (Gated PixelCNN, PixelCNN++) improved the receptive field (the plain stack has a blind spot to the upper right) and used a discretized logistic mixture output.

pythonmasked_conv.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class MaskedConv2d(nn.Conv2d):
    """Mask 'A': centre pixel excluded (first layer). Mask 'B': centre included (later layers)."""
    def __init__(self, mask_type, *args, **kw):
        super().__init__(*args, **kw)
        assert mask_type in ("A", "B")
        kH, kW = self.kernel_size
        mask = torch.ones_like(self.weight)                  # (out, in, kH, kW)
        mask[:, :, kH // 2, kW // 2 + (mask_type == "B"):] = 0   # centre row: block right of (or at) centre
        mask[:, :, kH // 2 + 1:, :] = 0                          # all rows below centre
        self.register_buffer("mask", mask)

    def forward(self, x):
        return nn.functional.conv2d(x, self.weight * self.mask, self.bias,
                                    self.stride, self.padding, self.dilation, self.groups)

# check causality: the output at position (i, j) must not depend on pixels at or after (i, j) for mask A
net = nn.Sequential(MaskedConv2d("A", 1, 8, 7, padding=3), nn.ReLU(), MaskedConv2d("B", 8, 8, 3, padding=1))
x = torch.randn(1, 1, 8, 8, requires_grad=True)
net(x)[0, :, 3, 4].sum().backward()
g = x.grad[0, 0] != 0
print("influenced pixels are all before (3,4) in raster order:", bool(g.flatten()[3 * 8 + 4:].sum() == 0))

WaveNet and audio

For audio the sequence is a waveform at 16-24 kHz, so a model needs huge receptive fields. WaveNet (van den Oord et al., 2016) uses stacks of dilated causal convolutions with dilation 1,2,4,…,5121,2,4,\dots,5121,2,4,…,512 repeated in blocks, so the receptive field grows exponentially with depth, gated activations, and a 256-way softmax over μ\muμ-law-quantized samples. It set the quality bar for text-to-speech but was painfully slow to sample (one network pass per audio sample); fast variants (Parallel WaveNet via distillation, WaveRNN, GAN vocoders) followed, and modern speech systems combine neural codecs that compress audio into discrete tokens with Transformers or diffusion models.

Transformers over tokens

Today autoregressive generation of images and audio usually works on discrete tokens from a learned tokenizer (VQ-VAE and VQ-GAN) rather than raw pixels, and uses a Transformer to model the token sequence. Examples: Image GPT (Chen et al., 2020, a GPT over low-resolution pixels), DALL-E (Ramesh et al., 2021, a Transformer over text tokens followed by image tokens), Parti (Yu et al., 2022), and audio models over neural-codec tokens. The tokenization trades pixel-level exactness for sequences short enough to model, and it lets all the language-model machinery (scaling laws, KV-cache, speculative decoding, RLHF) apply. The strengths are exact likelihood, a stable cross-entropy objective, scalability and a unified interface for multiple modalities. The weaknesses are slow, sequential sampling, an arbitrary ordering imposed on inherently 2-D data and error accumulation (exposure bias) in long sequences. Hybrid models such as masked-token generators (MaskGIT, Chang et al., 2022) decode many tokens in parallel in a few iterations, resembling diffusion on discrete tokens.

Comparing the generative families

You now have all the major families. The table compares them on the properties that decide which one to use. Ratings reflect the typical state of the art around 2023-2025 and are a guide, not a law: each family has been pushed beyond its stereotype by clever engineering.

VAE GAN Normalizing flow Autoregressive Diffusion / flow matching
Training objective ELBO (reconstruction + KL) minimax adversarial exact log-likelihood exact log-likelihood (cross-entropy) denoising regression (variational bound or reweighted)
Exact likelihood no (lower bound) no yes yes bound; exact via ODE (expensive)
Latent code yes, low-dim, learned encoder yes (no encoder) yes, same dimension, exact inverse none (tokens only) noise, deterministic via ODE
Sample quality blurry in pixel space sharp, fast moderate high (with tokens and scale) state of the art
Mode coverage good prone to collapse good good good
Sampling cost one pass one pass one pass DDD sequential passes (or tokens) 10-1000 passes (fewer with distillation)
Training stability stable unstable stable stable stable
Typical failure blur, posterior collapse mode collapse, instability poor fine detail, rigid architecture slow sampling, ordering artifacts slow sampling, high-guidance artifacts
Main uses today compression, latent spaces for other models real-time synthesis, super-resolution, vocoders, distillation targets density estimation, scientific sampling language, code, audio tokens, multimodal LLMs images, video, audio, 3D, molecules, robotics policies

A few observations for choosing in practice. If you need likelihoods (compression, anomaly detection, scientific models), prefer autoregressive models or flows. If you need real-time synthesis, prefer a GAN or a distilled diffusion model. If you want the best images and controllability, a latent diffusion model with guidance is the default. If you want one unified interface with language, an autoregressive Transformer is attractive. And note the convergence: latent diffusion uses a VAE; many tokenizers are VQ-VAEs trained with GAN losses; the best few-step samplers are adversarially distilled; diffusion Transformers borrow everything from language models. The families are components, not rival camps.

Applications

Diffusion-style generators are now general-purpose density learners for continuous signals, and a short survey shows how the ideas of this week recombine.

  • Images. Text-to-image systems (DALL-E 2, Imagen, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, and many others) combine a text encoder, latent diffusion and classifier-free guidance. Conditioning variants cover inpainting and outpainting, super-resolution (cascaded or latent), image editing by inversion and re-sampling (SDEdit, prompt-to-prompt), and fine-grained control (ControlNet, IP-Adapter-style image prompts, LoRA personalization such as DreamBooth).
  • Video. Video diffusion models add a time axis to the latent (3-D convolutions, temporal attention, or spacetime patches in a DiT), and are trained on enormous caption/video corpora; quality is limited by temporal consistency and the cost of long sequences, and many systems generate short clips and extend them.
  • Audio and music. Diffusion operates on spectrograms or on neural-codec latents (text-to-music, text-to-audio, speech synthesis); autoregressive token models remain strong competitors, especially for speech.
  • Science and engineering. Diffusion on 3-D coordinates and rotation groups for protein structure and molecule generation, conditional weather and trajectory generation, and diffusion policies for robot control (learning a distribution over action sequences). These connect directly to the geometric ideas of Week 14.
  • Inverse problems. Because a diffusion model is a learned prior, one can sample from the posterior p(x∣y)p(x\mid y)p(x∣y) for a measurement y=Ax+noisey=Ax+\text{noise}y=Ax+noise (denoising, deblurring, MRI reconstruction) by adding the measurement likelihood gradient to the score: the same decomposition as classifier guidance, with log⁡p(y∣xt)\log p(y\mid x_t)logp(y∣xt​) in place of log⁡p(c∣xt)\log p(c\mid x_t)logp(c∣xt​).

Risks, provenance and watermarking

High-quality, cheap generation changes the information environment, and responsible practitioners need to understand the technical facts as well as the ethics.

What can go wrong

  • Deepfakes and impersonation. Synthetic faces, voices and video of real people enable fraud (voice cloning in phone scams), harassment (non-consensual intimate imagery, a major real-world harm that disproportionately affects women), and political disinformation. A related harm is the "liar's dividend": real evidence can be dismissed as fake.
  • Training data, copyright and consent. Models are trained on web-scale images and text, many protected by copyright or containing personal data. The legal status varies by jurisdiction and is actively litigated; it is unresolved at the time of writing. Carlini et al. (2023) demonstrated that diffusion models can memorize and regurgitate individual training images, particularly ones duplicated many times in the data, which makes deduplication and membership audits a technical necessity, not only a legal one.
  • Bias and representation. Models reproduce and can amplify stereotypes present in training captions (occupations, nationalities, skin tones). Guidance makes prototypical (hence stereotypical) outputs more likely: a diversity-versus-fidelity trade-off with social consequences.
  • Misuse of open weights. Releasing weights enables research, auditing and local use, and also removes the ability to enforce safety filters. Safety classifiers, prompt filters, concept erasure and fine-tuning to remove a concept are partial mitigations; fine-tuning can usually undo them for open models.
  • Environmental and labor costs. Training and serving cost energy, and data labeling and content moderation rely on human work that is often poorly paid.

Detection, provenance and watermarking

Three technical ideas are used, each with different guarantees. Keep them separate.

  1. Passive detection trains a classifier to tell real from generated images using statistical artifacts. It works against the generators it was trained on and degrades on new generators, compression and editing: it is an arms race, and false positives (accusing a real photo) are costly. Treat a detector score as weak evidence.
  2. Content provenance (C2PA). The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity defines an open standard, "Content Credentials", for attaching cryptographically signed metadata to media: who or what produced it (a camera, an editing tool, a generative model), and a record of edits. Verification checks the signature chain. It does not detect fakes. It lets a trustworthy producer prove origin, and its absence means "unknown", not "fake". Weaknesses: metadata is easily stripped by screenshots or re-encoding, so it needs platform support and complementary signals (soft binding to a fingerprint or watermark) to survive.
  3. Watermarking. The generator embeds a signal in the output that survives common edits and can be detected by an algorithm. Post-hoc watermarks modify pixels or frequencies after generation. Generation-time watermarks are woven into the sampling process: for example, Tree-Ring watermarks (Wen et al., 2023) embed a pattern in the Fourier spectrum of the initial noise and detect it by inverting a (deterministic DDIM) sampler back to the noise; production systems such as Google DeepMind's SynthID embed imperceptible signals during generation. For language models, Kirchenbauer et al. (2023) bias token sampling toward a pseudo-random "green list". Limits: a watermark only identifies content from cooperating providers that embed it; adversaries can attempt removal (rewriting, regeneration, adding noise) or forgery; open-weight models can simply skip it.
A practical stance

No single technique solves authenticity. Defence in depth combines: signed provenance for content that wants to be trusted, watermarks for large providers' outputs, platform policy and labeling, legal and procedural norms (for example, consent requirements for synthetic likenesses), and user education. As an engineer, document training-data sources, evaluate memorization, red-team the system, log provenance metadata by default, and be clear about which claims your safeguards do and do not support.

Lab: a class-conditional DDPM on MNIST

You will build and train a small DDPM from scratch, conditioning on the digit label with classifier-free guidance, then run two experiments: number of sampling steps (DDPM vs DDIM) and guidance scale. A free Colab GPU trains it in 5-10 minutes (about 10 epochs); a CPU works but is slow. Fix a single device and seed at the top and keep every tensor on it.

Part 1: the diffusion process

pythonlab_diffusion.py
import math, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
torch.manual_seed(0)

def extract(a, t, x_shape):
    """Pick a[t] for each batch element and reshape to broadcast against x of shape x_shape."""
    out = a.gather(0, t)                                   # (B,)
    return out.view(-1, *([1] * (len(x_shape) - 1)))       # (B, 1, 1, 1)

class Diffusion:
    def __init__(self, T=1000, schedule="linear", device=device):
        self.T = T
        if schedule == "linear":
            betas = torch.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)
        elif schedule == "cosine":
            s = 0.008
            u = torch.arange(T + 1) / T
            f = torch.cos((u + s) / (1 + s) * math.pi / 2) ** 2
            ab = f / f[0]
            betas = (1 - ab[1:] / ab[:-1]).clamp(max=0.999)
        else:
            raise ValueError(schedule)
        betas = betas.double()
        alphas = 1.0 - betas
        ab = torch.cumprod(alphas, 0)
        ab_prev = torch.cat([torch.ones(1, dtype=torch.double), ab[:-1]])
        f32 = lambda v: v.float().to(device)
        # index i (0-based) corresponds to step t = i + 1 in the notation of the text
        self.betas, self.alphas, self.ab, self.ab_prev = f32(betas), f32(alphas), f32(ab), f32(ab_prev)
        self.post_var = f32(betas * (1 - ab_prev) / (1 - ab))      # beta_tilde_t

    def q_sample(self, x0, t, noise=None):
        """x_t = sqrt(ab) x0 + sqrt(1-ab) eps (the closed form)."""
        if noise is None:
            noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
        return extract(self.ab, t, x0.shape).sqrt() * x0 + extract(1 - self.ab, t, x0.shape).sqrt() * noise, noise

    def loss(self, model, x0, y):
        t = torch.randint(0, self.T, (x0.shape[0],), device=x0.device)
        x_t, eps = self.q_sample(x0, t)
        return F.mse_loss(model(x_t, t, y), eps)                    # L_simple

diff = Diffusion()
x0 = torch.randn(4, 1, 28, 28, device=device)
t = torch.tensor([0, 100, 500, 999], device=device)
x_t, eps = diff.q_sample(x0, t)
print("x_t shape:", x_t.shape, "| signal fraction sqrt(ab):", diff.ab[t].sqrt().tolist())
print("var of x_t at t=999:", x_t[-1].var().item())                 # ~ 1 (pure noise)

Part 2: the network

pythonlab_unet.py
import math, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class SinusoidalEmb(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__(); self.dim = dim
    def forward(self, t):                                            # t: (B,) integer steps
        half = self.dim // 2
        freqs = torch.exp(-math.log(10000.0) * torch.arange(half, device=t.device) / half)
        args = t.float()[:, None] * freqs[None, :]
        return torch.cat([args.sin(), args.cos()], dim=1)            # (B, dim)

class ResBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c_in, c_out, emb_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.n1 = nn.GroupNorm(8, c_in);  self.c1 = nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1)
        self.emb = nn.Linear(emb_dim, c_out)
        self.n2 = nn.GroupNorm(8, c_out); self.c2 = nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, padding=1)
        self.skip = nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 1) if c_in != c_out else nn.Identity()
    def forward(self, x, emb):
        h = self.c1(F.silu(self.n1(x)))
        h = h + self.emb(F.silu(emb))[:, :, None, None]              # inject timestep + label
        h = self.c2(F.silu(self.n2(h)))
        return h + self.skip(x)

class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(8, c); self.qkv = nn.Conv2d(c, 3 * c, 1); self.proj = nn.Conv2d(c, c, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        B, C, H, W = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.norm(x)).reshape(B, 3, C, H * W).transpose(2, 3).unbind(1)   # each (B, HW, C)
        o = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q[:, None], k[:, None], v[:, None])[:, 0]         # (B, HW, C)
        return x + self.proj(o.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, C, H, W))

class UNet(nn.Module):
    """28x28 -> 14x14 -> 7x7 -> back. Input channel 1. Labels 0..9 plus null label 10."""
    def __init__(self, ch=64, n_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        emb = ch * 4
        self.t_mlp = nn.Sequential(SinusoidalEmb(ch), nn.Linear(ch, emb), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(emb, emb))
        self.y_emb = nn.Embedding(n_classes + 1, emb)                 # last index = null condition
        self.inc = nn.Conv2d(1, ch, 3, padding=1)
        self.d1 = ResBlock(ch, ch, emb);          self.ds1 = nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, stride=2, padding=1)         # 28 -> 14
        self.d2 = ResBlock(ch, 2 * ch, emb);      self.ds2 = nn.Conv2d(2 * ch, 2 * ch, 3, stride=2, padding=1)  # 14 -> 7
        self.m1, self.ma, self.m2 = ResBlock(2 * ch, 2 * ch, emb), SelfAttention(2 * ch), ResBlock(2 * ch, 2 * ch, emb)
        self.us1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2), nn.Conv2d(2 * ch, 2 * ch, 3, padding=1))   # 7 -> 14
        self.u1 = ResBlock(4 * ch, 2 * ch, emb)                       # concat with skip from d2
        self.us2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2), nn.Conv2d(2 * ch, ch, 3, padding=1))       # 14 -> 28
        self.u2 = ResBlock(2 * ch, ch, emb)                           # concat with skip from d1
        self.out = nn.Sequential(nn.GroupNorm(8, ch), nn.SiLU(), nn.Conv2d(ch, 1, 3, padding=1))
        nn.init.zeros_(self.out[-1].weight); nn.init.zeros_(self.out[-1].bias)   # start by predicting 0

    def forward(self, x, t, y):
        emb = self.t_mlp(t) + self.y_emb(y)                           # (B, 4ch)
        h0 = self.inc(x)                                              # (B, ch, 28, 28)
        h1 = self.d1(h0, emb)                                         # (B, ch, 28, 28)
        h2 = self.d2(self.ds1(h1), emb)                               # (B, 2ch, 14, 14)
        m = self.m2(self.ma(self.m1(self.ds2(h2), emb)), emb)         # (B, 2ch, 7, 7)
        u = self.u1(torch.cat([self.us1(m), h2], 1), emb)             # (B, 2ch, 14, 14)
        u = self.u2(torch.cat([self.us2(u), h1], 1), emb)             # (B, ch, 28, 28)
        return self.out(u)                                            # (B, 1, 28, 28): predicted noise

net = UNet()
print(sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters()) / 1e6, "M parameters")
x = torch.randn(5, 1, 28, 28); t = torch.randint(0, 1000, (5,)); y = torch.randint(0, 11, (5,))
print(net(x, t, y).shape)                                             # torch.Size([5, 1, 28, 28])

Part 3: training with condition dropout and an EMA

pythonlab_train.py
import copy, torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
# assumes Diffusion, UNet, device from the previous parts (and drop_condition from cfg_core.py)

NULL_LABEL = 10
def drop_condition(y, p_uncond=0.1):
    mask = torch.rand(y.shape[0], device=y.device) < p_uncond
    return torch.where(mask, torch.full_like(y, NULL_LABEL), y)

tf = transforms.Compose([transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))])   # pixels to [-1, 1]
train = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True, transform=tf)
loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, drop_last=True, num_workers=2)

diff = Diffusion(T=1000, schedule="linear")
model = UNet().to(device)
ema = copy.deepcopy(model).eval().requires_grad_(False)                # exponential moving average of weights
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-4)

@torch.no_grad()
def ema_update(ema, model, decay=0.999):
    for pe, pm in zip(ema.parameters(), model.parameters()):
        pe.lerp_(pm, 1 - decay)                                        # pe = decay * pe + (1 - decay) * pm

for epoch in range(10):
    model.train(); total = 0.0
    for x0, y in loader:
        x0, y = x0.to(device), drop_condition(y.to(device))
        loss = diff.loss(model, x0, y)
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step(); ema_update(ema, model)
        total += loss.item()
    print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d}  mean loss {total / len(loader):.4f}")   # roughly 0.05-0.03 and slowly falling
torch.save(ema.state_dict(), "ddpm_mnist_ema.pt")

The loss is a mean-squared error on unit-variance noise: at initialization (predicting zero) it equals about 1.0, and it should drop quickly to a few hundredths. Do not expect it to keep falling dramatically: the irreducible part (the noise at high ttt that truly cannot be predicted) sets a floor, which is why sample quality, not loss, is the metric you must look at.

Part 4: samplers (DDPM and DDIM) with guidance

pythonlab_sample.py
import torch
# assumes Diffusion `diff`, trained EMA model `ema`, device, NULL_LABEL

@torch.no_grad()
def eps_guided(model, x, t, y, w):
    if w == 1.0:
        return model(x, t, y)
    e_c, e_u = model(torch.cat([x, x]), torch.cat([t, t]), torch.cat([y, torch.full_like(y, NULL_LABEL)])).chunk(2)
    return e_u + w * (e_c - e_u)

@torch.no_grad()
def sample_ddpm(model, diff, y, w=1.0, shape=(1, 28, 28), seed=0):
    """Ancestral sampling, T network evaluations (uses sigma_t^2 = beta_tilde_t)."""
    g = torch.Generator(device=y.device).manual_seed(seed)
    x = torch.randn(len(y), *shape, device=y.device, generator=g)
    for i in reversed(range(diff.T)):
        t = torch.full((len(y),), i, device=y.device, dtype=torch.long)
        eps = eps_guided(model, x, t, y, w)
        mean = (x - diff.betas[i] / (1 - diff.ab[i]).sqrt() * eps) / diff.alphas[i].sqrt()
        noise = torch.randn(x.shape, device=y.device, generator=g) if i > 0 else 0.0
        x = mean + diff.post_var[i].sqrt() * noise
    return x.clamp(-1, 1)

@torch.no_grad()
def sample_ddim(model, diff, y, steps=50, w=1.0, eta=0.0, shape=(1, 28, 28), seed=0):
    """DDIM over a subsequence of `steps` timesteps. eta = 0 is deterministic."""
    g = torch.Generator(device=y.device).manual_seed(seed)
    x = torch.randn(len(y), *shape, device=y.device, generator=g)
    ts = torch.linspace(diff.T - 1, 0, steps).round().long().tolist()          # e.g. 999, ..., 0
    for j, i in enumerate(ts):
        t = torch.full((len(y),), i, device=y.device, dtype=torch.long)
        eps = eps_guided(model, x, t, y, w)
        ab_t = diff.ab[i]
        ab_s = diff.ab[ts[j + 1]] if j + 1 < len(ts) else torch.tensor(1.0, device=y.device)   # alpha_bar at the next step
        x0 = ((x - (1 - ab_t).sqrt() * eps) / ab_t.sqrt()).clamp(-1, 1)         # clip the x0 estimate to the data range
        eps = (x - ab_t.sqrt() * x0) / (1 - ab_t).sqrt()                       # re-derive eps consistent with the clipped x0
        sigma = eta * ((1 - ab_s) / (1 - ab_t)).sqrt() * (1 - ab_t / ab_s).clamp(min=0).sqrt()
        noise = torch.randn(x.shape, device=y.device, generator=g) if eta > 0 else 0.0
        x = ab_s.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - ab_s - sigma ** 2).clamp(min=0).sqrt() * eps + sigma * noise
    return x.clamp(-1, 1)

ema.load_state_dict(torch.load("ddpm_mnist_ema.pt", map_location=device)); ema.to(device)
y = torch.arange(10, device=device).repeat_interleave(8)                       # 8 samples of each digit
imgs = sample_ddim(ema, diff, y, steps=50, w=3.0)
from torchvision.utils import save_image
save_image((imgs + 1) / 2, "samples_ddim50_w3.png", nrow=8)
print(imgs.shape, imgs.min().item(), imgs.max().item())

Part 5: experiments

Experiment A: steps. Compare DDIM at 5, 10, 20, 50 and 200 steps and DDPM at 1000 steps, with the same seed (so the same starting noise), at w=1w=1w=1. Look at the grids first, then measure quality with the quick classifier below. Expect: with 5 steps images are blobby; at 20-50 DDIM steps digits are clearly legible; DDPM at 1000 steps is the quality reference but 20-50 times slower.

Experiment B: guidance. Fix 50 DDIM steps and sweep w∈{0,1,2,4,8}w\in\{0,1,2,4,8\}w∈{0,1,2,4,8}. Expect w=0w=0w=0 (unconditional) to ignore the label, w=1w=1w=1 to follow it mostly, and w≥4w\ge4w≥4 to make digits bolder and more uniform in style (less diversity), with artifacts and saturation by w=8w=8w=8.

pythonlab_eval.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
# assumes sample_ddim, sample_ddpm, ema, diff, device from the previous parts

# 1) a tiny MNIST classifier (about 99% test accuracy after 3 epochs) to judge sample legibility
tf = transforms.Compose([transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))])
tr = DataLoader(datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, transform=tf), batch_size=256, shuffle=True)
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10)).to(device)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(clf.parameters(), 1e-3)
for _ in range(3):
    for x, y in tr:
        loss = F.cross_entropy(clf(x.to(device)), y.to(device)); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
clf.eval()

# 2) metrics on 500 samples per setting: label accuracy and within-class diversity
@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(sampler, n_per_class=50, **kw):
    y = torch.arange(10, device=device).repeat_interleave(n_per_class)
    imgs = sampler(ema, diff, y, **kw)
    acc = (clf(imgs).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()
    flat = imgs.flatten(1).view(10, n_per_class, -1)
    div = torch.stack([torch.pdist(c).mean() for c in flat]).mean().item()   # mean pairwise L2 within class
    return acc, div

for steps in [5, 10, 20, 50, 200]:
    acc, div = evaluate(sample_ddim, steps=steps, w=1.0)
    print(f"DDIM {steps:4d} steps   accuracy {acc:.3f}   diversity {div:.2f}")
for w in [0, 1, 2, 4, 8]:
    acc, div = evaluate(sample_ddim, steps=50, w=float(w))
    print(f"guidance w={w}   accuracy {acc:.3f}   diversity {div:.2f}")

You should see class accuracy rise with www (from chance, about 0.1, at w=0w=0w=0) and saturate near 1, while the diversity number falls: the same trade-off as the toy chart above. If accuracy at w=1w=1w=1 is already near 1, push the model harder by training for fewer epochs, or compare at w=0.5w=0.5w=0.5.

Common mistakes and debugging tips

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Samples are pure noise or grey blobs, loss barely moves from 1.0 data not scaled to [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], so the signal-to-noise assumptions break; or timestep not passed to the network normalize with mean 0.5, std 0.5; check t enters every block
Loss is fine, samples are very over-saturated or burnt sampler uses wrong indices (off-by-one between 0-based arrays and ttt in 1..TTT), or a missing clamp of x^0\hat x_0x^0​ print ab[0] and ab[T-1]; use the same index convention in training and sampling; clamp x^0\hat x_0x^0​ to the data range
Samples bright or dim on average, never very dark or light non-zero terminal SNR: model trained with αˉT>0\bar\alpha_T>0αˉT​>0 and sampled from pure noise zero-terminal-SNR rescaling plus vvv-prediction; or at least a schedule with αˉT≈0\bar\alpha_T\approx0αˉT​≈0
Guided samples ignore the label the null label was never used in training (no condition dropout), or sampling uses the wrong null index p_uncond about 0.1; same NULL_LABEL in train and sample; check ϵc≠ϵ∅\epsilon_c\ne\epsilon_\varnothingϵc​=ϵ∅​
Guided samples saturated, texture-less guidance scale too high; high-guidance artifacts lower www, apply guidance only in mid-trajectory, rescale or threshold x^0\hat x_0x^0​
DDIM with few steps looks worse than expected timestep subsequence skipped the high-noise region, or eta nonzero with few steps include t=T−1t=T-1t=T−1, space steps evenly (or in log-SNR), use η=0\eta=0η=0 for few steps
Training spikes or diverges high learning rate, no gradient clipping, or a bad init lr about 1e-4 to 2e-4, clip grad norm to 1, zero-init the output layer, use an EMA for sampling
EMA model gives worse samples than the raw model early on EMA decay too slow relative to the number of steps use decay=0.99 for short runs or warm up the decay; always sample from the EMA once it has seen enough steps
Different results on every run despite a fixed seed sampling noise from the global RNG or non-deterministic ops pass a torch.Generator to every randn (as in the lab)
Latent diffusion produces blurry or banded images wrong latent scaling factor, or the decoder is too weak scale latents to unit variance; check the autoencoder's reconstructions first
Memory blow-up in attention at higher resolution self-attention at 32x32 or 64x64 maps (N2N^2N2 cost) use attention only at 16x16 or lower; use flash attention; use latent diffusion

A general debugging habit: test the pieces separately. (1) Check that q_sample with t=0t=0t=0 returns almost the input and with t=T−1t=T-1t=T−1 is almost pure noise. (2) Overfit a single mini-batch: loss should fall far below the usual floor. (3) Evaluate the denoiser by plotting x^0\hat x_0x^0​ at several fixed ttt, which shows blurry means at high noise and sharp digits at low noise. (4) Use the toy exact-score sampler of this page to validate your sampler code, since it removes the network as a source of error.

Exercises

Exercise 1: variance preservation and the closed form

(a) Show that if xt−1x_{t-1}xt−1​ has mean mmm and variance vvv per coordinate, then xtx_txt​ has mean αt m\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,mαt​​m and variance αtv+βt\alpha_t v+\beta_tαt​v+βt​. (b) Use this to show that if the data have unit variance and zero mean, then every xtx_txt​ has zero mean and unit variance. (c) For data with variance σ02\sigma_0^2σ02​ and mean m0m_0m0​, find the mean and variance of xtx_txt​ in terms of αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​.

Solution

(a) xt=αtxt−1+βtϵx_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilonxt​=αt​​xt−1​+βt​​ϵ with ϵ\epsilonϵ independent: mean αtm\sqrt{\alpha_t}mαt​​m, variance αtv+βt\alpha_tv+\beta_tαt​v+βt​. (b) With m=0m=0m=0, v=1v=1v=1: variance =αt+βt=1=\alpha_t+\beta_t=1=αt​+βt​=1 at every step, by induction. (c) By the closed form xt=αˉtx0+1−αˉtϵx_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilonxt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ: mean αˉtm0\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}m_0αˉt​​m0​, variance αˉtσ02+1−αˉt\bar\alpha_t\sigma_0^2+1-\bar\alpha_tαˉt​σ02​+1−αˉt​. This tends to 111 as αˉt→0\bar\alpha_t\to0αˉt​→0 regardless of σ0\sigma_0σ0​, but it only equals 1 at every step if σ0=1\sigma_0=1σ0​=1. This is why data are normalized before diffusion and why latent-diffusion systems rescale their latents.

Exercise 2: where is the signal-to-noise ratio equal to one?

Using the NumPy code of the forward process, find the first step ttt at which SNR(t)<1\mathrm{SNR}(t)<1SNR(t)<1 (i.e. αˉt<0.5\bar\alpha_t<0.5αˉt​<0.5) for the linear schedule and for the cosine schedule with T=1000T=1000T=1000. What does the result say about how each schedule spends its steps?

Solution

For the linear schedule, np.argmax(ab < 0.5) + 1 returns t=260t=260t=260 (αˉ260≈0.4976\bar\alpha_{260}\approx0.4976αˉ260​≈0.4976). For the cosine schedule the crossing is at t≈497t\approx497t≈497, almost exactly the midpoint. So the linear schedule reaches equal signal and noise power after only a quarter of the steps and then spends the remaining three quarters (SNR from 1 down to 4×10−54\times10^{-5}4×10−5) on very noisy inputs, where the network has little to work with. The cosine schedule is much more evenly spread (see the log-SNR chart). This is the quantitative argument for the cosine schedule on small images.
