Exercise 4: the optimal denoiser for Gaussian data (derivation)

Let x0∼N(0,σ02)x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_0^2)x0​∼N(0,σ02​) in one dimension. (a) Find the marginal of xtx_txt​. (b) Find the optimal noise predictor ϵ∗(xt,t)=E[ϵ∣xt]\epsilon^*(x_t,t)=\E[\epsilon\mid x_t]ϵ∗(xt​,t)=E[ϵ∣xt​] and the score ∇log⁡pt\nabla\log p_t∇logpt​, and verify that ϵ∗=−1−αˉt ∇log⁡pt\epsilon^*=-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla\log p_tϵ∗=−1−αˉt​​∇logpt​. (c) Verify Tweedie's formula for E[x0∣xt]\E[x_0\mid x_t]E[x0​∣xt​].

Solution

(a) xt∼N(0,vt)x_t\sim\mathcal N(0,v_t)xt​∼N(0,vt​) with vt=αˉtσ02+1−αˉtv_t=\bar\alpha_t\sigma_0^2+1-\bar\alpha_tvt​=αˉt​σ02​+1−αˉt​. (b) xtx_txt​ and ϵ\epsilonϵ are jointly Gaussian with Cov(xt,ϵ)=1−αˉt\mathrm{Cov}(x_t,\epsilon)=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}Cov(xt​,ϵ)=1−αˉt​​, so E[ϵ∣xt]=1−αˉtvtxt\E[\epsilon\mid x_t]=\frac{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}{v_t}x_tE[ϵ∣xt​]=vt​1−αˉt​​​xt​. The score is ∇log⁡pt(xt)=−xt/vt\nabla\log p_t(x_t)=-x_t/v_t∇logpt​(xt​)=−xt​/vt​, so −1−αˉt∇log⁡pt=1−αˉt xt/vt-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\nabla\log p_t=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t/v_t−1−αˉt​​∇logpt​=1−αˉt​​xt​/vt​, matching. (c) E[x0∣xt]=αˉtσ02vtxt\E[x_0\mid x_t]=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\sigma_0^2}{v_t}x_tE[x0​∣xt​]=vt​αˉt​​σ02​​xt​ from the joint Gaussian with Cov(xt,x0)=αˉtσ02\mathrm{Cov}(x_t,x_0)=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\sigma_0^2Cov(xt​,x0​)=αˉt​​σ02​. Tweedie: (xt+(1−αˉt)(−xt/vt))/αˉt=xt vt−(1−αˉt)vtαˉt=xtαˉtσ02vtαˉt\big(x_t+(1-\bar\alpha_t)(-x_t/v_t)\big)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}=x_t\,\frac{v_t-(1-\bar\alpha_t)}{v_t\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}=x_t\frac{\bar\alpha_t\sigma_0^2}{v_t\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}(xt​+(1−αˉt​)(−xt​/vt​))/αˉt​​=xt​vt​αˉt​​vt​−(1−αˉt​)​=xt​vt​αˉt​​αˉt​σ02​​, identical. Note also what it says: at high noise (vt→1v_t\to1vt​→1) the best guess of x0x_0x0​ shrinks to the data mean; at αˉt→1\bar\alpha_t\to1αˉt​→1 it returns xtx_txt​.

Exercise 5: v-prediction conversions (coding)

Starting from the parameterizations.py code, train a tiny MLP to denoise a 2-D two-moons dataset with each of the three targets (ϵ\epsilonϵ, x0x_0x0​, vvv) on the linear schedule. For each, report the final loss, and the error in x^0\hat x_0x^0​ for 100 test points at t=50t=50t=50, t=500t=500t=500 and t=950t=950t=950. Which target gives the most uniform behavior across ttt, and why?

Solution

A reference implementation: build x_t with the closed form, feed [x_t, t/T] to a 3-layer MLP, regress the chosen target with MSE, and for evaluation convert the output to x^0\hat x_0x^0​ with to_x0. Typical outcome: ϵ\epsilonϵ-prediction gives small x^0\hat x_0x^0​ errors at low ttt but large ones at t=950t=950t=950 (the conversion divides by αˉt≈0.04\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\approx0.04αˉt​​≈0.04, amplifying network error by about 25); x0x_0x0​-prediction is best at high ttt but blurry at low ttt (it must recover fine noise-free detail from a nearly clean input without ever being told which part is noise); vvv is the most uniform, since by Exercise 3 its implied x0x_0x0​-weight 1+SNR1+\mathrm{SNR}1+SNR never vanishes and never explodes relative to the target scale. Your numbers will vary with seed and architecture; check the trend, not the absolute values.

Exercise 6: classifier-free guidance on a toy problem (coding, challenging)

Reproduce the guidance chart. Use the exact-score machinery of ddim_toy_exact_score.py with two classes N(−1,0.82)N(-1,0.8^2)N(−1,0.82) and N(+1,0.82)N(+1,0.8^2)N(+1,0.82), the unconditional model being their equal-weight mixture and the conditional model the single Gaussian of class B. Sample with 100-step DDIM and ϵ~=ϵ∅+w(ϵc−ϵ∅)\tilde\epsilon=\epsilon_\varnothing+w(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_\varnothing)ϵ~=ϵ∅​+w(ϵc​−ϵ∅​) for w∈{0,1,2,4,8}w\in\{0,1,2,4,8\}w∈{0,1,2,4,8}. (a) Report the sample mean and standard deviation. (b) Explain why the mean at w=8w=8w=8 exceeds the class mean +1+1+1. (c) What would the guided density be if both classes were exactly separated and Gaussian with the same variance? Derive it.

Solution
python
import numpy as np
T = 1000
ab = np.concatenate([[1.0], np.cumprod(1 - np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T))])
mc, sc = np.array([-1.0, 1.0]), 0.8

def eps_star(x, k, mus, sigs, wts):
    a = ab[k]; m = np.sqrt(a) * mus[None, :]; v = a * sigs**2 + 1 - a
    lp = np.log(wts)[None, :] - 0.5 * (x[:, None] - m) ** 2 / v - 0.5 * np.log(v)
    p = np.exp(lp - lp.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return np.sqrt(1 - a) * (p * (x[:, None] - m) / v).sum(1)          # = -sqrt(1-ab) * score

def run(w, n=100, N=20000, seed=2):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); ks = np.round(np.linspace(T, 0, n + 1)).astype(int)
    x = rng.standard_normal(N)
    for t, s in zip(ks[:-1], ks[1:]):
        ec = eps_star(x, t, mc[1:], sc, np.array([1.0]))               # class B only
        eu = eps_star(x, t, mc, sc, np.array([.5, .5]))                # unconditional mixture
        e = eu + w * (ec - eu)
        x0 = (x - np.sqrt(1 - ab[t]) * e) / np.sqrt(ab[t])
        x = np.sqrt(ab[s]) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - ab[s]) * e
    return x.mean(), x.std()

for w in [0, 1, 2, 4, 8]:
    print(w, run(w))

(a) Approximately: w=0w=0w=0: mean 0.01, std 1.26 (the unconditional mixture); w=1w=1w=1: mean 1.00, std 0.78 (class B); w=2w=2w=2: 1.51, 0.57; w=4w=4w=4: 2.08, 0.45; w=8w=8w=8: 2.79, 0.38. (b) The guided density is ∝p(x) p(B∣x)w\propto p(x)\,p(B\mid x)^w∝p(x)p(B∣x)w. Since p(B∣x)p(B\mid x)p(B∣x) is a logistic function of xxx that keeps increasing toward x→+∞x\to+\inftyx→+∞, raising it to a large power drags mass toward larger xxx, away from the class boundary and past the class mean: guidance optimizes "how clearly class B" and not "how typical of class B". (c) For p(x)=12N(μA,σ2)+12N(μB,σ2)p(x)=\tfrac12\mathcal N(\mu_A,\sigma^2)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(\mu_B,\sigma^2)p(x)=21​N(μA​,σ2)+21​N(μB​,σ2) the guided density p(x∣B)wp(x)1−wp(x\mid B)^w p(x)^{1-w}p(x∣B)wp(x)1−w for www greater than 1 is not Gaussian: with well-separated classes the term p(x)1−wp(x)^{1-w}p(x)1−w is a negative power of a mixture, which is large between and outside the modes. In the region near mode B, p(x)≈12p(x∣B)p(x)\approx\frac12 p(x\mid B)p(x)≈21​p(x∣B), so the density is ∝p(x∣B) (1/2)1−w\propto p(x\mid B)\,(1/2)^{1-w}∝p(x∣B)(1/2)1−w: nearly unchanged. So for well-separated classes guidance does almost nothing; it matters exactly when the classes overlap, which is the regime of real images and text.

Exercise 7: is DDIM marginal-preserving? (what-if)

Take Gaussian data N(0,σ02)N(0,\sigma_0^2)N(0,σ02​) with σ0=2\sigma_0=2σ0​=2 and the exact optimal ϵ∗\epsilon^*ϵ∗ from Exercise 4. Apply one deterministic DDIM step (η=0\eta=0η=0) from αˉt=0.3\bar\alpha_t=0.3αˉt​=0.3 to αˉs=0.6\bar\alpha_s=0.6αˉs​=0.6. Compute the variance of the output and compare with the target marginal variance αˉsσ02+1−αˉs=2.8\bar\alpha_s\sigma_0^2+1-\bar\alpha_s=2.8αˉs​σ02​+1−αˉs​=2.8. Repeat with αˉs=0.35\bar\alpha_s=0.35αˉs​=0.35 and 0.3010.3010.301. What do you conclude?

Solution

With ϵ∗=1−αˉt x/vt\epsilon^*=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x/v_tϵ∗=1−αˉt​​x/vt​ and x^0=αˉtσ02x/vt\hat x_0=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\sigma_0^2x/v_tx^0​=αˉt​​σ02​x/vt​, the step is linear: xs=c xx_s=c\,xxs​=cx with c=(αˉtαˉsσ02+(1−αˉt)(1−αˉs))/vtc=\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t\bar\alpha_s}\sigma_0^2+\sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha_t)(1-\bar\alpha_s)}\big)/v_tc=(αˉt​αˉs​​σ02​+(1−αˉt​)(1−αˉs​)​)/vt​. Output variance c2vtc^2v_tc2vt​: for αˉs=0.6\bar\alpha_s=0.6αˉs​=0.6 it is 2.6082.6082.608 (target 2.82.82.8); for 0.350.350.35, 2.0442.0442.044 (target 2.052.052.05); for 0.3010.3010.301, 1.90301.90301.9030 (target 1.90301.90301.9030 to four digits). A single large DDIM step does not preserve the marginal; the error shrinks quickly (roughly quadratically in the step size) as s→ts\to ts→t, where DDIM becomes the exact probability-flow ODE. This is why few-step sampling has an error floor, why higher-order solvers help, and why the "DDIM 1000 steps" line in the chart plateaus above Monte Carlo noise.

Exercise 8: change of variables and coupling layers

(a) A 1-D flow is x=az+bx=az+bx=az+b with z∼N(0,1)z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)z∼N(0,1). Compute log⁡pX(x)\log p_X(x)logpX​(x) by the change-of-variables formula and check it against the Gaussian density. (b) For the affine coupling layer with x∈R2x\in\R^2x∈R2, y1=x1y_1=x_1y1​=x1​, y2=x2es(x1)+t(x1)y_2=x_2e^{s(x_1)}+t(x_1)y2​=x2​es(x1​)+t(x1​), write the Jacobian and its determinant. (c) Why would using s(x1,x2)s(x_1,x_2)s(x1​,x2​) in place of s(x1)s(x_1)s(x1​) break the efficiency of the layer?

Solution

(a) f(x)=(x−b)/af(x)=(x-b)/af(x)=(x−b)/a, ∣f′∣=1/∣a∣|f'|=1/|a|∣f′∣=1/∣a∣, so log⁡pX(x)=log⁡N((x−b)/a;0,1)−log⁡∣a∣=−12(x−b)2a2−12log⁡2π−log⁡∣a∣\log p_X(x)=\log\mathcal N\big((x-b)/a;0,1\big)-\log|a|=-\tfrac12\frac{(x-b)^2}{a^2}-\tfrac12\log2\pi-\log|a|logpX​(x)=logN((x−b)/a;0,1)−log∣a∣=−21​a2(x−b)2​−21​log2π−log∣a∣, which is the log-density of N(b,a2)\mathcal N(b,a^2)N(b,a2). (b) J=(10∂y2/∂x1es(x1))J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \partial y_2/\partial x_1&e^{s(x_1)}\end{pmatrix}J=(1∂y2​/∂x1​​0es(x1​)​), det⁡J=es(x1)\det J=e^{s(x_1)}detJ=es(x1​), log⁡∣det⁡J∣=s(x1)\log|\det J|=s(x_1)log∣detJ∣=s(x1​). (c) With s(x1,x2)s(x_1,x_2)s(x1​,x2​) the entry ∂y2/∂x2\partial y_2/\partial x_2∂y2​/∂x2​ would pick up a x2 ∂s/∂x2x_2\,\partial s/\partial x_2x2​∂s/∂x2​ term, and the map would no longer be invertible in closed form (solving y2=x2es(x1,x2)+ty_2=x_2e^{s(x_1,x_2)}+ty2​=x2​es(x1​,x2​)+t for x2x_2x2​ is an implicit equation); the Jacobian would stop being triangular with an easy diagonal. The whole point of coupling is that s,ts,ts,t depend only on the unchanged half.

Exercise 9: what would happen if...

(a) You trained a conditional diffusion model with puncond=0p_\text{uncond}=0puncond​=0 and then sampled with w=3w=3w=3 using a null label. (b) You trained with puncond=0.9p_\text{uncond}=0.9puncond​=0.9. (c) You used BatchNorm instead of GroupNorm in the U-Net and sampled one image at a time at inference. (d) You sampled a model trained for T=1000T=1000T=1000 steps using only the timesteps {999,500,0}\{999, 500, 0\}{999,500,0} with DDIM.

Solution

(a) The null embedding is an untrained, random vector; ϵ∅\epsilon_\varnothingϵ∅​ is then an arbitrary extrapolation and guided samples are corrupted (typically artifacts or noise-like images). Guidance needs both tasks to be trained. (b) The conditional model sees the label only 10% of the time and learns it poorly; guidance can compensate partly (the unconditional branch is excellent), but the conditional branch is weak, so prompt fidelity is bad and you waste capacity. Typical values are 0.05 to 0.2. (c) BatchNorm statistics at training time come from batches of mixed noise levels and at inference from a batch of one at one noise level: train/test mismatch gives poor samples, and it couples samples within a batch. GroupNorm and LayerNorm are per-sample. (d) Three steps is far too coarse: the model has an error floor (Exercise 7 and the chart, 3-step error of about 0.63 versus 0.02 at 1000 steps) and the result would be blurry digit-like blobs. The first step from pure noise to the model's x^0\hat x_0x^0​ is essentially the posterior mean, the blurry average of all digits.

Exercise 10: the probability-flow ODE (derivation, challenging)

Using the Fokker-Planck equation ∂tpt=−∇⋅(fpt)+12g2Δpt\partial_tp_t=-\nabla\cdot(fp_t)+\tfrac12g^2\Delta p_t∂t​pt​=−∇⋅(fpt​)+21​g2Δpt​ for dx=f dt+g dWdx=f\,dt+g\,dWdx=fdt+gdW, show that the deterministic ODE x˙=f−12g2∇log⁡pt\dot x=f-\tfrac12g^2\nabla\log p_tx˙=f−21​g2∇logpt​ has the same marginals ptp_tpt​. Then explain why the reverse SDE has drift f−g2∇log⁡ptf-g^2\nabla\log p_tf−g2∇logpt​ but the ODE uses only half of the score term.

Solution

Use Δp=∇⋅∇p=∇⋅(p ∇log⁡p)\Delta p=\nabla\cdot\nabla p=\nabla\cdot(p\,\nabla\log p)Δp=∇⋅∇p=∇⋅(p∇logp). Then ∂tpt=−∇⋅(fpt)+12g2∇⋅(pt∇log⁡pt)=−∇⋅([f−12g2∇log⁡pt]pt)\partial_tp_t=-\nabla\cdot\big(fp_t\big)+\tfrac12g^2\nabla\cdot(p_t\nabla\log p_t)=-\nabla\cdot\Big(\big[f-\tfrac12g^2\nabla\log p_t\big]p_t\Big)∂t​pt​=−∇⋅(fpt​)+21​g2∇⋅(pt​∇logpt​)=−∇⋅([f−21​g2∇logpt​]pt​). This is the continuity (Liouville) equation for a deterministic flow with velocity f~=f−12g2∇log⁡pt\tilde f=f-\tfrac12g^2\nabla\log p_tf~​=f−21​g2∇logpt​, so particles following x˙=f~\dot x=\tilde fx˙=f~​ have marginals ptp_tpt​. For the reverse-time SDE with noise ggg we need two things: time reversal flips the sign of the drift of the (forward) diffusion contribution, and the stochastic term itself diffuses mass; to cancel that diffusion and reverse the density evolution we need an extra score term. Concretely, running the Fokker-Planck equation backward for a process with diffusion ggg requires the full g2∇log⁡ptg^2\nabla\log p_tg2∇logpt​, half of which is "undoing" the diffusion that the added noise g dWˉg\,d\bar WgdWˉ does again. In the ODE there is no noise term to undo, so half the score is sufficient. In general one can interpolate: dx=[f−1+λ22g2∇log⁡pt]dt+λg dWˉdx=\big[f-\tfrac{1+\lambda^2}{2}g^2\nabla\log p_t\big]dt+\lambda g\,d\bar Wdx=[f−21+λ2​g2∇logpt​]dt+λgdWˉ has marginals ptp_tpt​ for any λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0 (with λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 the ODE and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 the reverse SDE), which is the continuous analogue of DDIM's η\etaη.

Exercise 11: provenance, watermarking and detection

You are asked to design the authenticity strategy for a photo-generation product. (a) What does a C2PA manifest prove, and what does it fail to prove? (b) Name two ways a watermark can fail. (c) Why is a classifier-based "AI image detector" a poor sole basis for moderation or academic-integrity decisions?

Solution

(a) It proves that a specific signing party (identified by a certificate chain) asserted particular claims (capture device, edits, generation tool) about a particular asset hash, and that the asset and manifest have not been modified since signing. It does not prove the claims are true (a signer could lie), does not survive stripping (absence of a manifest tells you nothing), and does not detect fakes made without it. (b) Removal or degradation by re-generation, heavy compression, cropping, noise or paraphrase attacks (an adversary with access to the detector may optimize against it), and non-adoption (open-weight models and other providers simply do not embed one); also forgery of a watermark on real content if the key leaks. (c) Detectors have non-zero false-positive rates that hit real people (and have shown bias against some groups, for example non-native writers for text detectors), they generalize poorly to new generators and edits, and their scores are not calibrated for individual decisions. Use them as one weak signal alongside provenance and human review.

Key takeaways

Key takeaways
  • Diffusion has a fixed forward noising chain and a learned reverse chain. The closed form xt=αˉtx0+1−αˉt ϵx_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilonxt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ϵ turns training into cheap regression at a random noise level.
  • The ELBO is a sum of KLs between Gaussians; with the ϵ\epsilonϵ-parameterization it reduces to weighted noise prediction, and dropping the weights (Lsimple\mathcal L_\text{simple}Lsimple​) improves samples but is no longer a likelihood bound.
  • ϵ\epsilonϵ-, x0x_0x0​- and vvv-prediction are linear reparameterizations of each other; they differ in implicit loss weighting (SNR versus 1+1+1+SNR versus 1) and numerical conditioning. vvv-prediction behaves well at every noise level.
  • The network is a score estimator: sθ=−ϵθ/1−αˉts_\theta=-\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}sθ​=−ϵθ​/1−αˉt​​. Denoising score matching gives the loss; the reverse SDE and the deterministic probability-flow ODE generate samples from it.
  • DDIM and higher-order ODE solvers reduce 1000 steps to 10-50 because the probability-flow trajectory is smooth; distillation and consistency training go lower by changing the model.
  • Classifier-free guidance, ϵ~=ϵ∅+w(ϵc−ϵ∅)\tilde\epsilon=\epsilon_\varnothing+w(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_\varnothing)ϵ~=ϵ∅​+w(ϵc​−ϵ∅​), samples from p(x)p(c∣x)wp(x)p(c\mid x)^wp(x)p(c∣x)w: higher fidelity and prompt adherence, lower diversity, artifacts at large www.
  • Latent diffusion runs diffusion in a VAE latent space (48 times fewer values at f=8f=8f=8) with cross-attention to text tokens; U-Nets and DiTs are interchangeable denoisers, DiTs scale predictably.
  • Flows give exact likelihood through invertible layers with cheap Jacobians (coupling layers); autoregressive models factorize by the chain rule and now operate on learned tokens. Each family trades quality, likelihood, speed and stability differently.
  • Generative media bring real risks (deepfakes, memorization, bias). Provenance (C2PA), watermarking and detection are complementary and none is sufficient alone.

Essential

  • Ho, Jain and Abbeel, "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models", NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv:2006.11239). The paper that made diffusion practical: read the forward process, the simplified loss and the U-Net.
  • Song, Sohl-Dickstein, Kingma, Kumar, Ermon and Poole, "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations", ICLR 2021 (arXiv:2011.13456). The SDE/ODE unification.
  • Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser and Ommer, "High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models", CVPR 2022 (arXiv:2112.10752). The basis of Stable Diffusion.
